World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Authorities capture CJNG leader, Navy backs US $115M sargassum strategy and Kia commits $649M to EVs
World.content:
The week of July 27th in Mexico ended with a major security win as agents captured the alleged intellectual author of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo’s assassination, a case that rattled Michoacán, a state burdened by organized crime, in late 2025.

President Claudia Sheinbaum, meanwhile, spent much of the week swatting away rhetorical grenades lobbed from abroad: she rejected Argentine President Javier Milei’s claim that Mexico was funding an “anti-Argentina campaign,” and brushed off White House adviser Stephen Miller’s assertion that cartels control Mexico’s political system, telling reporters the United States “must look at itself” on drug consumption. Closer to home, a cheating scandal consumed Mexico’s largest and most prestigious university, which confronted suspicions that AI and old-fashioned cheat sheets had corrupted its admissions exam. In a lighter moment, chefs in the capital’s Venustiano Carranza borough assembled a 100-meter, 1.5-tonne torta at the International Torta Fair, a Guinness-certified spectacle that drew hundreds of thousands of visitors.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Mastermind of Manzo murder captured in Jalisco

Federal authorities on Thursday arrested Ramón Ángel “R1” Álvarez Ayala, the alleged mastermind behind the November 2025 assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Álvarez Ayala, leader of a CJNG-linked cell known as “Los R’s,” was apprehended in Atotonilco, Jalisco, in an operation involving a high-speed chase and a shootout that left one of his bodyguards dead. García Harfuch later detailed R1’s criminal history, noting he was first jailed in 2012 for orchestrating a wave of violence in Guadalajara, was released in 2022, and resumed criminal activity soon after — allegedly ordering several killings, including that of influencer Valeria Márquez. His capture marks the 31st arrest connected to Manzo’s murder, a killing that shocked Mexico’s political and business classes and turned the independent mayor into a national symbol of local officials’ vulnerability to organized crime.

Mexicans now view China more favorably than the US, Pew finds

A new Pew Research Center survey found that Mexicans view China more favorably than the United States for the first time in nearly two decades of polling. Some 59% of Mexican respondents said they had a favorable opinion of China, compared to 40% for the U.S., and Mexicans were roughly three times more likely to express confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping than in Donald Trump. Canada showed a similar reversal, and Pew noted the trend held across most of the 36 countries it surveyed. Analysts attribute the shift largely to worsening views of Washington rather than improving perceptions of Beijing, with younger Mexican adults especially likely to favor China over the U.S.

Chemical spill near Arizona border triggers emergency response

Two separate freight train derailments prompted emergency responses over the weekend. In Ciudad Madero, Tamaulipas, authorities declared a Code Red and evacuated more than 200 residents after a Pemex-owned tank car carrying 70,000 liters of gasoline tipped over in a rail yard.

Farther north, a Ferromex freight train derailed in Naco, Sonora, spilling roughly 59,000 liters of sodium hydrosulfide, a corrosive chemical used in copper mining, just south of the U.S. border. Heavy rain then hampered cleanup efforts in Sonora, forcing families near the Cuauhtémoc ejido to temporarily leave their homes due to fumes. Sonora’s Civil Protection Agency said emergency measures were deployed immediately, while the National Water Commission is testing water and soil to determine whether the chemical reached waterways near Cananea. The Federal Attorney General’s Office has opened an investigation into the derailment, which occurred on a Grupo México-linked rail line and raised fresh concerns about industrial safety in a state that is already home to some of Mexico’s largest copper mining operations.

Del Toro caps historic Tour de France

Cyclist Isaac del Toro delivered Mexico’s best-ever Tour de France result, finishing third overall and taking the white jersey as the race’s best young rider — a result celebrated by President Sheinbaum. The 22-year-old from Ensenada, Baja California, made history early in the three-week race too, winning Stage 2 in Barcelona after teammate and four-time champion Tadej Pogačar eased up in the final meters to let the young rider take the victory, a gesture that left Del Toro visibly stunned. It was the first Tour stage win by a Mexican rider in 36 years, since Raúl Alcalá’s back-to-back victories in 1989 and 1990. Del Toro’s final-week performance in the Alps, where Pogačar again worked to protect his young teammate’s position, sealed a podium finish that surpassed Alcalá’s previous best of eighth place, cementing Del Toro’s status as Mexico’s greatest cyclist and a genuine contender for future Grand Tours.

Acapulco hydroelectric dam project scrapped

Sheinbaum canceled the long-controversial La Parota dam project near Acapulco, citing unresolved land expropriation issues and a lack of community agreements. In its place, the government will build radial wells along the Papagayo River, rehabilitate aqueducts and replace drinking water lines serving the city’s upper neighborhoods.

Foreign investment keeps flowing

Several new investment announcements underscored continued foreign interest in Mexico.

Houston-based Talos Energy agreed to acquire a 50% stake in Repsol’s offshore Block 29 in the Gulf of Mexico, home to the Polok and Chinwol oil discoveries.

South Korean automaker Kia announced a US $649 million investment to begin producing its EV3 electric SUV at its Pesquería, Nuevo León plant starting Aug. 4 — the model’s first production site outside South Korea, expected to create 500 jobs this year and 1,500 more by 2030.

On the consumer side, U.S. cookie chain Crumbl opened its first Mexico store in Roma Norte, CDMX, to 800-person lines, while gourmet hot dog chain Dog Haus debuted in Mérida, part of a broader wave of American food brands expanding south.

Mexican economy shows signs of life

The MND Economy Index™, a 10-pillar composite gauge of Mexico’s economic health, rose to 68.61 in its latest edition — its highest reading yet, driven by improving inflation and monetary policy scores even as economic growth remains the weakest-performing pillar. The improving picture was reinforced by other data this week:

Mexico’s export revenue hit a record US $389.72 billion in the first half of 2026, a 24.6% annual increase driven by a surge in non-automotive manufacturing exports.

The economy grew 1.5% quarter-over-quarter in Q2, Mexico’s best result since late 2020, aided by World Cup-related tourism spending.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard also weighed in on the trade relationship with Washington, downplaying Trump’s latest remark that he “doesn’t care” about the USMCA. “Obviously there are warnings every week, there are a lot of things,” Ebrard told reporters, adding that “as of today we’re doing well.” Sheinbaum echoed the sentiment, noting the two countries’ economies remain deeply integrated after decades of free trade.

Navy presents US $115M sargassum plan

With Quintana Roo facing its worst sargassum season on record, the Mexican Navy announced a 2-billion-peso plan to combat the seaweed influx choking Caribbean coast beaches. The strategy includes roughly 50 kilometers of new anti-sargassum sea barriers near Playa del Carmen, Cancún, Tulum, Puerto Morelos and Mahahual, along with new collection vessels aimed at eventually processing 4,000 tonnes of sargassum per day. Quintana Roo has already collected more than 92,000 tonnes of the macroalgae this year, with officials projecting the total could exceed 119,000 tonnes before year’s end.

World Bank aligns support with Plan México

World Bank Group President Ajay Banga made his first visit to Mexico in five years, meeting with Sheinbaum to align a new five-year Country Partnership Framework with the government’s Plan México industrial strategy. The framework will prioritize infrastructure, energy, water management and human capital development.

Banga also toured Grupo Naturasol, a family-owned agribusiness in México state that previously received International Finance Corporation financing, calling it a model for how smaller firms can plug into North American supply chains.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: When legacy media’s hypocrisy gets called out: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
I am increasingly finding myself analyzing the Mexico narrative as it’s told by different media outlets. Just this past week brought us another ludicrous example with The Atlantic magazine publishing an article titled “A Planeload of Informants” with the subtitle: “The United States is intensifying its hunt for narcos within the Mexican government. Is this all prelude to an attack?”

I guess The Atlantic was feeling left out of the party by other large media outlets writing breathtakingly sensationalist articles about Mexico. If you remember, leading up to the World Cup, The Economist magazine informed its readers that: “The World Cup will test Mexico’s control over its territory.” The Wall Street Journal told us that the “World Cup puts Mexico’s Cartel Crisis on the Global Stage.” And the New York Times has written at length of experts confidently predicting Mexico would enter a period of increasing violence after the February government operation against CJNG leader Mencho.

But they have all been wrong. Totally wrong. The post-Mencho spiral of violence? It didn’t happen. In fact, Mexico has seen its homicide rates hitting lows not seen in over a decade. The “World Cup test” of Mexico against the cartels? There was no test. The world watched with envy as foreigners partied alongside Mexicans across the country. Not a single article has been written acknowledging getting things so wrong. And so now we have the media moving on to the next big story: A potential attack by the United States on Mexico.

Let’s be clear about the history here: Mexico has, for decades, genuinely struggled with cartel violence, and I am not arguing otherwise. But what these outlets consistently omit is the context of the last year. Cooperation between the U.S. and Mexico against cartels is, in the words of officials on both sides, at unprecedented levels — a shift I’ve tracked in real time (see my columns on the World Cup coverage and Mexico’s business community). The result of that cooperation isn’t more violence; it’s homicides down by almost 50% this year. Apparently good news doesn’t sell subscriptions.

Which brings me to two personal anecdotes from this past week that I want to share:

Cancelling a 30-year subscription

The first took place at a friend’s dinner party in Mexico City. A few hours into some good conversation, he (quite randomly) asked me: “Do you still read The Economist magazine?” To which I responded that I do. He then said: “I have been a loyal subscriber for over 30 years, but I am about to cancel it. I am done with them.” His reasoning was enlightening: “I am tired of the narrative of their coverage. By cancelling my subscription with them, I am choosing to not pay attention to the reality that they are presenting.” He went on: “The predictive power of their writers and editors has changed … and as a result they are just flat out wrong on many topics.”

The words stuck with me as I have been increasingly feeling the same about The Economist. In just the past few months, I have actually written twice about how intellectually lazy, disingenuous and downright wrong their coverage has been regarding Mexico. Increasingly, as I read their coverage on the country, I have found myself wondering, “Why am I reading this? It’s not accurate. It’s sensationalist. And it doesn’t represent reality. Why am I paying to read something that I think is just plain wrong?”

As my friend’s cancellation shows, his decision reflects a broader pattern I’m seeing: As irresponsible coverage piles up, readers simply stop trusting — and stop paying for — outlets they once considered essential.

The conversation went further with others at the party explaining that, in contrast, they read Mexico News Daily precisely because it “provides optimism by showing me the Mexico that I want to believe exists today and believe can exist in the future.” The comment wasn’t made out of ignorance or a lack of information, but rather in a way that reinforced the optimism they have for Mexico. Said differently, they are choosing to align with a narrative of informed optimism versus colonialist click-bait pessimism. It’s unfortunate to increasingly see people tuning out of legacy media, but it’s easy to understand why they are doing it. As many outlets increasingly present a pessimistic, dystopian, doom-and-gloom view of much of the world — one that increasingly is out of touch with reality — many people are choosing to tune out.

The Economist’s Elon Musk interview

The second anecdote came earlier this week when I watched The Economist’s editor-in-chief, Zanny Minton Beddoes, interview Tesla/SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. The nearly 90-minute-long interview went on fine for the first hour, but then turned decidedly testy. Ms. Beddoes at one point begins to take issue with Musk’s assessment of the current state of the U.K. (where The Economist is based and where she lives). She questioned his motives, repeatedly said he was incorrect, accused him of supporting “fringe” and “far right” parties and questioned when he had last visited the U.K. To be clear, the point here is not whether Musk’s take on the U.K. is right or wrong, that’s a separate debate entirely.

Here you have the head of The Economist, the British publication that has increasingly misconstrued, misrepresented and irresponsibly presented other countries around the world, getting extremely defensive about someone questioning the U.K. She repeatedly took offense to any of Musk’s critiques of her own country, claiming “People say that you’re racist,” “people loathe you,” “What is the motivation for [participating in tribalism]?” It was quite shocking to see the head of a publication that for decades has portrayed much of the rest of the world as dangerous, backwards and corrupt take so much offense to someone questioning the current state and future direction of her own country.

As she waged increasingly personal attacks against Musk, he finally had enough and responded with a dagger: “A lot more people hate you, the media — more than you realize. Do you realize the media is despised? Do you realize … the favorable view of journalists is like 15%? … They hate you.” It was a striking moment. Her defensiveness made her and her publication feel small, out of touch, aloof. It was a moment where I found myself even further questioning the true motives of The Economist.

Musk’s jab about journalism’s approval rating isn’t just a soundbite — it’s the direct consequence of the pattern I described above. When outlets choose sensationalism over accuracy, they erode trust in journalism broadly, pushing people toward sources — credible or not — that at least feel honest to them.

Is The Economist really trying to live by its founding mission from 179 years ago of taking part “in a severe contest between intelligence, which presses forward, and an unworthy, timid ignorance obstructing our progress”? Or are they more likely contributing to the obstruction of progress with increasingly ignorant and biased journalism? If the latter is in fact the case, as I sadly suspect it is, they will likely experience more people like my friend moving on.

I strongly believe that the role of the media is more important than ever. But we in the media also needs to work harder than ever to earn your trust and respect — and many outlets seem to have forgotten that.

Thank you for reading and supporting MND.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: ‘War With Me And The Mother-In-Law’: Man charged with trying to light mother-in-law’s house on fire with her in it
World.content:
‘War With Me And The Mother-In-Law’: Man charged with trying to light mother-in-law’s house on fire with her in it

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 22-year-old construction worker accused of deliberately setting fires inside his former mother-in-law’s Belize City home has pleaded not guilty to two counts of arson in the High Court.

Sir Hugh Anthony Andrewin appeared unrepresented before Justice Nigel Pilgrim this week, where he was formally indicted on the two charges.

Justice Pilgrim strongly advised Andrewin to obtain an attorney, telling him that the allegations against him were “very serious offences.” The judge gave him approximately three months to seek legal representation and adjourned the matter until November 13, 2026.

Andrewin was further remanded to the Belize Central Prison, as he also has other pending matters before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court for which he remains on remand.

The charges arise from two alleged incidents at a home on Flamboyant Street on June 11 and June 12, 2025.

Police allege that at about 10:00 p.m. on June 11, Andrewin arrived at the residence of his now former mother-in-law, pulled out a blue lighter and set fire to a sheet covering a grey loveseat valued at $400. The woman reportedly extinguished the fire before it could spread further.

Several hours later, at about 4:00 a.m. on June 12, the woman and her daughter were reportedly awakened by smoke and found a curtain and a green loveseat valued at $750 engulfed in flames. The fire also damaged aluminium louvre windows valued at $495.

The prosecution alleges that the second fire was set with the intention of endangering both women. Andrewin initially faced one arson charge in the Magistrate’s Court but was indicted on two counts when the matter reached the High Court.

World.title: Village man sent to jail after police bust him riding up-stop in Belize City
World.content:
Village man sent to jail after police bust him riding up-stop in Belize City

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Lords Bank construction worker was sent to prison for two weeks after his arrest for riding a bicycle against the flow of traffic led the court to uncover several unpaid fines for previous bicycle offences.

Ashton Keiron Garbutt appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court and pleaded guilty to causing a bicycle to proceed along a one-way street in the wrong direction.

Police alleged that at about 1:30 a.m. on Sunday, July 26, 2026, cops saw Garbutt riding against traffic on Vernon Street.

According to the officers, Garbutt jumped from the bicycle and hid behind a vehicle after noticing the police. He was searched, but nothing illegal was found.

When informed of the traffic offence, Garbutt reportedly told the officers, “Boss man, I nuh know this dah one way because I dah nuh from here; I dah from village.”

During his arraignment, Garbutt told the court that it was his first traffic conviction. However, a check of his court record showed that he had five previous traffic convictions, including offences for riding bicycles without bells or lights in 2020 and 2021. The magistrate reprimanded him for being untruthful.

Garbutt was fined $30, along with $5 in court costs, for the latest offence. He was given until August 10, 2026, to pay or serve one month in prison.

However, the court also discovered that Garbutt owed $105 in fines from five previous traffic convictions. When he was unable to pay the outstanding amount immediately, a warrant was issued and he was escorted to the Belize Central Prison to serve two weeks.

All of Garbutt’s previous bicycle-related convictions reportedly arose from incidents within Belize City.

World.title: Belize City man fined $360 for assaulting ex-girlfriend and throwing her phone in the drain but must compensate ex $200; Relationship advice from the Judge: ‘Let it go’
World.content:
Belize City man fined $360 for assaulting ex-girlfriend and throwing her phone in the drain but must compensate ex $200; Relationship advice from the Judge: ‘Let it go’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man was fined and ordered to compensate his former girlfriend after admitting that he assaulted her and threw her cellphone into a drain during a domestic dispute.

Francis Staine, 30, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he pleaded guilty to common assault and damage to property.

Police alleged that on Monday, July 27, 2026, Staine assaulted the woman and damaged her cellphone by throwing it into a drain. The dispute reportedly arose after Staine accused her of being unfaithful.

While the complainant described Staine as her ex-boyfriend, he told the court that they had still been in a relationship up until the incident. He also said their child was with the woman at the time.

In mitigation, Staine became emotional and described himself as a hardworking person.

“I can give her back the phone, and I promise I will leave her alone,” he told the court.

The court advised Staine to accept that the relationship had ended and “let it go.” Staine acknowledged that he needed to move on and leave the woman alone.

He was fined a total of $360 for the two offences and ordered to pay the complainant $200 in compensation for the damaged cellphone by September 30, 2026. Failure to pay the compensation could result in distress proceedings against him.

World.title: Belize City messenger fined $155 for possession of crack pipe
World.content:
Belize City messenger fined $155 for possession of crack pipe

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City messenger received his first drug-related conviction after pleading guilty to possession of a crack pipe.

Alexander Rodolfo Chan, 37, of Antelope Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court this week, where he admitted to possession of a pipe.

Police alleged that Chan was found with a metal pipe on June 24, 2026. The object had reportedly been used or adapted for smoking crack cocaine.

In mitigation, Chan asked the court to impose a fine rather than a custodial sentence. The court considered that he was a first-time offender with no previous drug-related convictions.

Chan was fined $150, along with $5 in court costs. He was given until August 31, 2026, to pay the total amount or serve two weeks in prison.

World.title: Minister’s cleaner fined $155 after after being busted with crack pipe
World.content:
Minister’s cleaner fined $155 after after being busted with crack pipe

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City cleaner was fined on Friday after pleading guilty to possession of a pipe used for smoking crack cocaine.

Kareem Duane Young, 40, of Freetown Road, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on a single charge of possession of a pipe.

Police alleged that Young was found on Mapp Street on Saturday, July 26, 2026, with a black pipe that had been used or adapted for smoking crack cocaine or another controlled drug.

Young, who told the court that he works as a cleaner for a government minister, admitted that the pipe belonged to him and that he used it to smoke crack cocaine.

He was fined $150, along with $5 in court costs. Young was given until August 31, 2026, to pay the total amount or serve two weeks in prison.

World.title: ‘Drink Water And Mind Your Business’: Man fined $150 for throwing stones at neighbor’s house but he says he was just trying to alert them there was an intruder in the yard
World.content:
‘Drink Water And Mind Your Business’: Man fined $150 for throwing stones at neighbor’s house but he says he was just trying to alert them there was an intruder in the yard

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City handyman was fined on Friday after pleading guilty to throwing missiles at a home on Black Orchid Street.

Kenyon Kareem Dominguez, 34, a self-employed handyman from the Lake Independence area, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he admitted to throwing objects at the residence of a neighbor.

Dominguez was fined $150, along with $5 in court costs. He was given until September 30, 2026, to pay the amount or serve two weeks in prison.

In court, Dominguez explained that he had noticed someone allegedly lurking in the yard and threw small pebbles at the house in an attempt to wake the occupants and alert them.

“I was trying to alert them that an intruder was in their yard. Instead of hollering, I threw pebbles to wake them,” Dominguez told the court.

He expressed regret over the incident, saying he should not have interfered and should have minded his own business. Dominguez had also spent the weekend in police custody before being taken to court.

World.title: ‘F**k The Police’: Hattieville man sentenced to three years for busting several shots at police officer with illegal gun
World.content:
‘F**k The Police’: Hattieville man sentenced to three years for busting several shots at police officer with illegal gun

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 24-year-old Hattieville man who probably listen to too much NWA was sentenced to three years in prison on Friday after admitting that he fired several shots at a police officer who approached him while he was carrying a firearm in public.

Blake Norman Lewis appeared unrepresented before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he changed his previous not-guilty pleas to guilty for keeping an unlicensed firearm, aggravated assault upon a police officer and discharging a firearm in public.

The charges arose from an incident on February 8, 2026, when a cop reportedly saw Lewis walking along a Hattieville street carrying what appeared to be a firearm.

Rivero told investigators that he contacted the Hattieville Police Station for backup but received no response. When he approached Lewis and identified himself as a police officer, Lewis allegedly raised the weapon and opened fire.

The officer took cover and returned fire, while Lewis reportedly continued shooting before fleeing and leaving behind a silver pistol with an empty magazine. Ten expended shells were recovered from the scene.

Police later detained Lewis in the Sibun area with gunshot injuries to his foot and back. He was discharged from the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital on February 10 and handed over to the Queen Street Police Station.

Lewis had been on remand for approximately five months before changing his pleas. He was initially sentenced to four and a half years for the firearm offence, but deductions were made for his guilty plea, expressions of remorse, mitigation and time already spent on remand, leaving him with two years to serve on that charge.

He received an additional one-year sentence for aggravated assault, which will run consecutively. Another one-year sentence for discharging a firearm in public will run concurrently, bringing his total prison term to three years.

In mitigation, Lewis told the court, “I am sorry for what I did. I will never do it again.” He said he had remained positive while incarcerated and had participated in the ARC Programme, Journey to Freedom and other rehabilitation programmes.

Lewis’s uncle also spoke on his behalf, describing him as a calm individual, his mother’s “right hand” and a loving father who frequently spoke about his children. He asked the court for leniency and suggested that Lewis be allowed to pay a fine.

Senior Magistrate Dennison told Lewis that, at 24, he still had his entire life ahead of him and an opportunity to change. However, she said the court had to send a strong message that firing at police officers could not be tolerated.

World.title: Belize City man remanded on attempted murder charge following Berkeley Street stabbing
World.content:
Belize City man remanded on attempted murder charge following Berkeley Street stabbing

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 32-year-old Belize City man was remanded to the Belize Central Prison on Friday after being charged in connection with the stabbing of Charles Myles during an altercation earlier this week.

Byron Jeffords, an unemployed resident of Wagner’s Lane, appeared unrepresented before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison, where he was read charges of attempted murder, dangerous harm and use of deadly means of harm.

No plea was taken because the offences are indictable, and Jeffords was informed that the Magistrate’s Court could not grant him bail at this stage.

During the arraignment, Jeffords began telling the court, “I acted in self-defence,” and attempted to show the magistrate an injury to his left pinky finger. However, the magistrate cautioned him against making further statements that could incriminate him while he was without legal representation.

Jeffords was remanded until September 30, 2026.

According to police, officers received a report of a fight on Berkeley Street at about 10:05 a.m. on Wednesday, July 29. Investigators later visited the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where Myles, a 26-year-old labourer of Wagner’s Lane, was being treated for an apparent stab wound to his back.

Initial investigations indicated that Myles and Jeffords were involved in an argument that escalated into a fight, during which Jeffords allegedly produced a sharp object and injured Myles.

Myles was transported to the hospital in a police mobile and was reported to be in stable condition. Scenes of Crime personnel processed and photographed the area where the stabbing reportedly occurred.

Jeffords was later detained and charged with the three offences.

World.title: Stronger than ganja!
World.content:
Consultant child and adolescent psychiatrist Dr Ganesh Shetty says child guidance clinics are now seeing more children addicted to digital devices than to marijuana. He has sounded an alarm over what he describes as a pattern of “disconnection and misconnection, alienation and addiction” amongst Jamaican youngsters.

“These algorithms are created by behavioural specialists, and they drag you into something more interesting, something more wonderful, so that it will suck you in to addiction. I have more tablet addicts coming to my child guidance clinics than weed addicts nowadays,” Dr Shetty disclosed as he warned minors of the danger courted daily.

There are 23 of these clinics in hospitals and health centres throughout Jamaica, providing mental health and counselling services for clients up to 18 years old. Key services include behavioural assessments, emotional support, and treatment for conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and depression.

It is unclear if the troubling trend has emerged at all of them.

Dr Shetty, who is also acting director, adolescent mental health, in the Ministry of Health, made the disclosure on digital device addiction during last week’s press conference to present findings of the National Study on Social Media Use and the Protection of Children.

He outlined the toll addiction takes.

“We have teenagers who are so disconnected [from] everybody and everything. And this is what happens when you’re disconnected, and misconnected, and addicted: You don’t sleep; you don’t eat; you’re miserable. Next day, nobody can talk to you, including your mom. And sometimes, when you see a lot of shooting and fighting and cutting off head and cutting off fingers on your screen, you get disconnected [from] that human suffering. So somebody gets hit in school [and you are more] interested in taking a video of it and putting it online so it can go viral — not going and assisting that person,” he pointed out.

Dr Shetty noted that the attraction to screens has its genesis in seemingly harmless choices made by parents and guardians during their children’s early years. He cited the example of a mother who gives her two-year-old an iPad when out in public to prevent the child from “running up and down”. The woman is proud of her baby who appears well-behaved and does not cause “discomfort to others and mother”.

The mental health professional then described a scenario in which the mother has two more children at home, absent fathers, and she uses digital devices to fill the gap as she does household chores such as cooking.

“So she has to have the older two watch some TV and the younger one to deal with the tablet. What happens? The child gets disconnected from the human beings around her/him, and gets connected with the machine and, even at this age, can get addicted to the machine,” Dr Shetty outlined.

He said a child’s affinity for his electronic device only grows, becoming a competitor for the time spent on every other aspect of life.

“It can affect you, affect your energy, affect your focus, affect your memory, affect your school grades, affect what you want to become. You can’t become [a success] because you don’t have grades to go to college, but you have just grades enough to go to supermarket and push cart,” he warned.

Dr Shetty is heartened that there is recognition that a holistic approach is needed to tackle the areas of concern outlined in the study, which is said to be “one of the most comprehensive national assessments ever undertaken” on social media use by minors in Jamaica.

“I’m glad that most folks you interviewed think it has to be done together. Government cannot do it alone. Community cannot do it alone. Family cannot do it alone. Young persons have to be involved in it. It is a family and community effort,” he said.

According to the study, nine out of every 10 respondents, or 90.2 per cent, support government regulation of minors’ social media use, while 2.9 per cent expressed opposition. Nearly 84 per cent believe Jamaica should establish a clear national policy framework governing minors’ use of social media.

World.title: Catherine Hall is back!
World.content:
President of the Montego Bay Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Jason Russell, on his way to winning the Celebrity Cook Off at Saturday’s staging of Montego Bay Jerk and Food Festival.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Local stakeholders are thrilled with the return of activities to Catherine Hall Entertainment Centre, with Saturday’s staging of Montego Bay Jerk and Food Festival, an annual event whose fate was in question after the venue was damaged by last October’s Hurricane Melissa.

“The feeling of being in this Catherine Hall Entertainment Centre is one of triumph,” president of the Montego Bay Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Jason Russell, told the Jamaica Observer on the sidelines of the celebrity chef cook-off competition which he later won.

“To see the park back and opened, separate and apart from Jerk Fest, to see the Government fix back the park, it looks good. The grass looks good, the walls are up, the fences are up. It gives me a real warm feeling and MoBay is really back,” he added.

Catherine Hall was among the hardest-hit sections of the city when the Category 5 storm struck and the popular entertainment venue was not spared. A section of its perimeter wall was washed away and although it has since been repaired, the venue remained unused for months. Its marquee event, Reggae Sumfest, went to St Ann on July 18 for a one-day event, scaling down the show from the usual seven days.

“They didn’t think that the park would be ready in time and being here we realise that some good work was done,” Russell stated.

Also in attendance at Saturday’s event was Mayor of Montego Bay Richard Vernon, who was equally pleased with the venue’s return.

“It’s good to know that the centre can be used for events. I was always of the view that it could be used ever since the hurricane, just needed to do a little work to get it back in order to ensure we can host events of this size. Today is testament to that thought process back then and we intend for the regular activities in this area to return,” he said.

The facility is owned and operated by the Urban Development Corporation (UDC), which the mayor said had been working diligently to restore the venue. He also commended organisers of Saturday’s event for successfully taking on the challenge of hosting a major event after the hurricane.

Promoter John Lindo admitted there had been significant concerns when organisers first assessed the venue which on Saturday was still being powered by generators. They decided to go ahead with the show, he said, as they did not want to disappoint regular patrons and they know how important the event is to the city.

“Montego Bay Jerk Festival is the people’s show. For 17 years we have been doing it and we must be doing something good. It is a clean, nice show. We do things straight and we do things right and so I guess that is why… the sponsors… are always coming back on board,” he said.

Several sponsors, he added, have thrown their support behind the usual plan to give back to the community by helping individuals connected to the festival and are Hurricane Melissa victims.

Lindo said once arrangements are finalised, organisers will identify the beneficiaries and determine the level of assistance to be provided.

For Mayor Vernon, however, the benefits of the festival were already evident Saturday, particularly for vendors operating both in and outside the venue.

“Events like these they provide spin-offs to other businesses and that is why they are so important. We work closely with promoters to give them as much support as possible to have these types of events,” he asserted.

“Some of them have houses damaged, they’re still fixing and at the same time, you have to send children back to school so they have to deal with that, so I am happy for this opportunity for them and I am happy for this opportunity for the city of Montego Bay,” he stated.

The festival attracted thousands of patrons despite an earlier threat of rain. Attendees enjoyed a wide variety of food, drinks and activities that culminated in a stage show featuring performances by songbird Alliance and several other artistes.

World.title: Pick up a book
World.content:
Kinloss Primary and Infant School teacher Shernette Brooks packing away books she received from Blue World Travel’s Festival at Sea delegation at the Falmouth Port last Wednesday.Horace Hines

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — Regional director at the Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) Odette Dyer is urging Jamaican children to spend less time on tablets and rediscover the joy of reading, describing books as one of the greatest investments that can be made in a child’s future.

“Please put away the tablets a little bit. That’s not your only avenue for learning and understanding the world. Open your minds to reading a book because when you read, it prepares you for learning, achieving and doing your schoolwork that much better,” Dyer urged students attending a ceremony where 1,000 children’s books were among items donated to 15 schools across Trelawny, St James, and St Elizabeth.

School supplies were also presented to the institutions through a partnership involving Blue World Travel — one of America’s leading travel companies for African American travellers — JTB, and local charity Sarah’s Children. The handover was done at the historic Falmouth Port during the arrival of Celebrity Cruise Lines’

Reflection, which was carrying a delegation from Blue World Travel’s annual Festival at Sea.

Dyer described every donated book as “an opportunity to spark imagination, encourage learning and inspire the dreams of a young Jamaican”. Recalling her childhood, the tourism player said books introduced her to the world long before she had the opportunity to travel.

“I am a testament to reading and loving books. Back then we didn’t have technology, and books sparked my curiosity to explore different cultures. Later, I experienced the world first-hand and was not disappointed,” she said.

Welcoming the visitors, Dyer thanked Blue World Travel President Patricia Nicholson Yarbrough and the team for once again selecting Jamaica as the beneficiary of the annual book drive.

“Tourism is at its best when it creates meaningful connections between people,” Dyer said, noting that initiatives such as the donation demonstrate tourism’s ability to enrich communities long after visitors have returned home. She also commended Festival at Sea passengers who packed books and school supplies before boarding the cruise.

Blue World Travel, a San Francisco-based agency that created Festival at Sea, America’s original African-American cultural cruise, has incorporated children’s book drives into the annual programme for more than three decades.

Yarbrough said the 34th Festival at Sea continued a tradition that began during the cruise’s second year.

“Our passengers are the ones who actually bought all of these books for the schools and libraries. We wanted to give something back to the islands that host us,” she said.

Former Los Angeles School District administrator Peggy Taylor Presley said about 85 per cent of the donated books feature Afro-centric characters, giving students the opportunity to see themselves reflected in the stories they read.

“You can be anything you want to be,” Presley told the students.

Sarah’s Charity Founder Janet Silvera said the donation was particularly meaningful in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, which damaged schools and learning resources across western Jamaica.

“For some institutions, rebuilding a library has become just as important as rebuilding a classroom,” she said, adding that every book has the potential to unlock imagination, build confidence and change a child’s future.

Among the beneficiaries was Kinloss Primary and Infant School in Trelawny.

Teacher Shernette Brooks said the donation would help establish a reading corner for the infant department while expanding the school’s library.

“The child-friendly books will support our younger learners, while the remaining books will benefit the wider student population,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Meanwhile, Dyer thanked the visitors for their generosity, friendship and belief in the potential of Jamaica’s children and encouraged them to experience Jamaica beyond the cruise port.

“Go out, explore the destination and engage with a Jamaican,” she urged.

World.title: No quarrel with the courts
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (second left) and president of the Jamaican Bar Association (Jambar) Tenneshia Watkins (second right) celebrate Jamaica’s first female Director of Public Prosecutions Paula Llewellyn (left) and former Jambar President Ian Wilkinson, both King’s Counsel, who were honoured Friday night during the association’s annual banquet.Joseph Wellington

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness, whose legal team on Friday lost an appeal to block the disclosure of certain files in his battle with the Integrity Commission (IC), later that evening reaffirmed the importance of an independent judiciary. While speaking broadly about his Administration and not directly referencing his legal issues, Holness stressed that he has no quarrel with the application of the law — even at times when it “constrains the actions of the executive”.

On the contrary, he stressed that “a strong and independent legal profession is indispensable to the rule of law”.

“It provides citizens with representation, assists the court in administering justice, scrutinises public authority, and helps ensure that rights are protected and obligations enforced. Jamaica has a constitutional order built deliberately on the separation of powers, and that separation will, from time to time, produce tension between the branches of the State. I say that as I see others smiling. I do not regard such tension as a defect in our democracy. I regard it as evidence that our democracy is working,” the prime minister declared.

He was speaking to an audience of leaders and other members of the justice system during the 2026 Jamaican Bar Association’s (Jambar) Annual Banquet.

It is essential, the prime minister said, for the judiciary to provide checks and balances.

“When the courts constrain the actions of the executive, they do not obstruct the work of the Government; they discharge the very duty the constitution assigns them. An executive that is never checked is an executive that has forgotten the source of its authority. And let me say that this executive has never forgotten the source of its authority,” added Holness.

He spoke of the importance of a judiciary that is impartial, and displays “principled application of the law” for all Jamaicans, not just some.

“We also expect this for all our citizens who seek access to the courts. That is what secures the confidence of our citizens in our Government and institutions, and this is what keeps us free as we pursue major reforms and investment in security, infrastructure, and the economy,” the prime minister said.

Critics have frowned upon Holness’s decision to take the IC to court. However, his proponents have consistently argued that it is his right — as it is for any other Jamaican — to seek legal redress.

The prime minister was granted leave by the Supreme Court in 2024 to apply for judicial review of the IC’s report on his statutory declarations, challenging processes engaged by the IC and its Director of Investigations Kevon Stephenson.

Holness has maintained that he has not broken the law since the tabling of the report that contained recommendations that the Financial Investigations Division (FID) and Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) examine his financial dealings.

He sought a declaration that the commission acted unfairly and unlawfully in its conduct of an investigation into his statutory declarations, with his lawyers arguing that the issues were of critical importance to the overall fairness of the proceedings. It was revealed, Friday, that their bid was unsuccessful.

Hours after, the prime minister spoke of the importance of a system of justice that is beyond reproach, framing his comments within a national context.

“Confidence in our legal system is essential. Investors and citizens must trust our laws, contracts, and institutions,” he told the audience of legal professionals from bench and bar.

During the banquet, Jamaica’s first female Director of Public Prosecutions Paula Llewellyn, and former Jambar President Ian Wilkinson, both King’s Counsel, were honoured. Wilkinson is also president of the Jamaica Chess Federation. The prime minister paid tribute to them both.

“They have demonstrated that excellence at the Bar requires much more than technical knowledge. It demands discipline, preparation, courage, integrity, and an abiding respect for institutions,” said Holness.

He also acknowledged a select group of legal stalwarts who were being honoured for individually giving five decades of service to the profession.

“Fifty years of advocacy, 50 years of counsel, 50 years of mentorship — most important — but 50 years of service! You have trained generations, preserved our traditions, and helped shape our institutions we rely on today. Jamaica owes you a debt of gratitude,” Holness said.

Reflecting on her journey from a young child to the peak of her profession as a public servant, Llewellyn was adamant that she would have it no other way.

“I learned from very early that when you have positions in life and you have to serve the people, do not levitate up into the clouds. Stay on the ground, serve the people, they will always know when you are sincere,” she urged young professionals present.

Wilkinson, for his part, emphasised the importance of hard work and mentorship to the craft while urging young professionals to aim for maximising their contributions to the legal arena and country, rather than seeking to line their pockets.

World.title: Four Caribbean countries affected as US$20,000 Visa Bond programme made permanent
World.content:
A Visa Bond Programme requiring nationals from specific countries to pay up to US$20,000 before being granted a United States (US) Visa will become permanent on August 3 after what the US government says is a successful pilot.

Four Caribbean countries – Cuba, Dominica, Grenada and Antigua and Barbuda – are included in the list of 50 countries.

The Antigua and Barbuda Government has already announced it is lobbying heavily for a rollback of the requirements for its citizens.

The programme was initially launched in 2025 in an effort to prevent overstaying.

The US State Department in a draft notice on Friday, revealed that the decision to make the rule permanent was taken after the programme “provided sufficient data to suggest that a visa bond program is an effective tool for enforcing compliance among bonded visa holders,” US media has reported.

The bond, which is returned to travellers once they exit the country on time, can be between US$10,000 to US$20,000 at the discretion of consular officers.

World.title: Rented, stripped, relisted
World.content:
Homeowners, prospective buyers, and renters are being urged to use real estate agents to minimise their risks.

AS short-term rental scams become more sophisticated, real estate expert Roger Allen is warning that fraudsters are misusing booking platforms like Airbnb in many ways, including renting homes then illegally listing them online without the property owners’ consent, and using fake listings to swindle unsuspecting customers.

The second vice-president of the Realtors Association of Jamaica (RAJ) said the extent of booking platforms-related fraud became apparent during a meeting with the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) last year, during which he and other members of the RAJ were briefed on numerous scams involving short-term rental properties.

“There are persons thinking that they have more or less rented a property or leased an Airbnb and, in terms of the payments, some of them are being urged to go outside of the platform to make payment and that sort of thing,” Allen told the Jamaica Observer.

He added that he is also aware of instances in which people rented a property listed on Airbnb, removed its furniture, then listed it for rent, bilking individuals out of thousands of dollars.

In a recent post on X, formerly Twitter, one user recounted how a woman she knew was allegedly defrauded of $190,000 through a similar scheme. According to the post, the woman signed a rental agreement and was given keys to the property, only to later discover that the house was an Airbnb rental and the individual who collected her deposit had no authority to rent it.

Allen said another emerging scam involves fraudsters renting properties legitimately before listing them on booking platforms as short-term vacation rentals without the owners’ knowledge or consent.

“In our space, in terms of the realtors in our groups…I could tell you that for last year 2025, even up to Christmas, I have seen and received information from members of over 20 instances. A number of them, I recall, have been reported…One of the things that we have found out, and the JCF has also said, is that from embarrassment and otherwise, given the circumstances of some of these situations, some of the property owners are just choosing to deal with the matter through their own ways, which again is not recommended because, as much as possible, persons need to be brought under the full book of the law,” he told the

Sunday Observer.

He noted that as these scams become increasingly sophisticated, real estate professionals are adapting their practices and strengthening verification measures to reduce the risk of fraud for both property owners and prospective tenants.

“One of the things we say to clients is that, ‘You may want to insist in the contract, in the lease agreement, that there’s no subletting of the property,’ because some of the persons even want to legitimately operate the property in short-term rentals and some of them will try to get in the property and not even disclose that if they’re going to sublet it,” said Allen.

He urged homeowners, prospective buyers, and renters to use real estate agents to minimise their risks.

“We are what you call licensed operators. We are licensed annually. It’s not that we get the licence when we do the certification and we have the licence for life. Every year we have to renew that licence, and importantly, we have continued professional development courses and other regulatory stuff in keeping with proceeds of crime, anti-money laundering, all these things, and not to mention strict guidelines in terms of the Real Estate [Dealers and] Developers Act in terms of how we operate,” insisted Allen.

He urged the public to keep an eye out for warning signs, noting that every realtor has a dealer number and a licence number that can be checked and verified. If these numbers are not displayed or an individual wants to confirm a realtors status, he said individuals can make checks to confirm the legitimacy of realtors at the Realtors Association of Jamaica website.

“Remember, scammers are looking for any and every opportunity to please persons. If you want to go and see a property, whether you want to lease it or whether you want to buy it, there is no deposit that is required. We do some vetting on all of that, but nothing like that in terms of collecting fees, so we want to alert the public in that regard,” he added.

World.title: ‘We are nowhere’
World.content:
Jamaicans must demand meaningful constitutional reform from the political directorate.

WITH Jamaica on the cusp of its 64th Independence celebrations, constitutional reform advocate Robert Stephens is urging the political directorate to end the politicisation of the country’s constitutional reform and establish an independent committee, headed by civil society, to chart the course towards Jamaica becoming a republic.

His call comes as the Government continues to blame the parliamentary Opposition for stalling the constitutional reform process, while Opposition Leader Mark Golding maintains that Jamaica’s transition to a republic should not proceed unless the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) replaces the United Kingdom-based Privy Council as the country’s final appellate court.

Stephens, a member of the Advocates Network, said the failure of the previous constitutional reform process indicates that a new committee needs to be established.

“It [the Constitutional Reform Committee] shouldn’t be led by a politician. It should be led by somebody from civil society, preferably a judge, and it should have members from the two major political parties, but also from civil society. Let us seriously move now towards establishing consensus on a new approach to a new constitution, which has to include the fact that we become far more independent from the king and the queen and the monarchy. The time has come for us to get serious because that last attempt…was totally unsuccessful,” said Stephens.

He stressed that when two political parties have differences of opinion, those differences cannot be easily resolved by having someone who is a member of one party head the committee.

“What you need is some independence, and there needs to be serious dialogue about how we’re going to move towards being a republic, and that requires public education and discussion, and involving the people of every parish of the island. The approach that was taken before was definitely not the right way to do it, where a politician was, as a minister, in charge of the whole committee, and then you had selected members, which were packed with people who were mainly government appointees. I think what you need is a far more independent group that is going to seriously address all of the shortcomings of our current constitution,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

He also questioned the value taxpayers have received from the constitutional reform exercise, pointing to the millions of dollars already allocated to the process despite little tangible progress.

“That’s unacceptable. The other thing is the headquarters for the previous ministry is sitting there locked up. Now, are we paying rent for that still? Taxpayers’ money is not something to be spent idly. Really and truly, we need far more responsive and responsible governance in terms of the way that our money is being handled,” said Stephens.

Weighing in on the topic, Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister Delroy Chuck argued that the Opposition is responsible for delaying the process after refusing to support the Constitution (Amendment) (Republic) Bill, 2024, unless it also includes provisions to replace the Privy Council with the CCJ. He called on the leader of the Opposition to resume the process.

Chuck said the Government had already conducted extensive public consultations through islandwide town hall meetings and believed there had been agreement on removing the British monarch before the Opposition altered its position.

“At the very last moment, the Opposition decided that they would not proceed unless the CCJ was decided on; that is what is holding up the process. There is no need to go back into any further discussion islandwide. As far as we are concerned, it’s a decision that has been held up by the Opposition.

“There might be a bit of tweaking as to how that president should be nominated and selected and approved. A Bill was put in Parliament, and all that is necessary is for it to be debated, and we move forward. Moving towards a republic has been decided on, but it has been inordinately delayed by the position of the Opposition,” Chuck told the Sunday Observer.

Providing an update on the progress made, Chuck said, “We are nowhere” as it relates to making Jamaica a republic.

“We have not moved for over a year now, so nothing really has been done. Everything is at a standstill because the Opposition is not prepared to move forward until the Government commits to joining the CCJ, which in my mind is most unfortunate on their part,” said the minister.

“There is no doubt that once we move forward with the republic, then we can again put a constitutional commission together to look at other areas of the constitution; that is not a problem. But, remember, we have just come out of a broad-based constitutional commission. Yes, you might not support everything they did, but at least there was consensus on moving forward with the republic, so let’s do that and not allow the work of the last constitutional commission to be totally wasted.

“If you don’t allow something to come out of it, then we may have another constitutional commission and nothing comes out of it,” Chuck stressed.

The Opposition leader has argued in several public statements and interviews that replacing the king as head of State without simultaneously adopting the CCJ would amount to only partial decolonisation.

“The Opposition’s position has been consistent. We are not in favour of a piecemeal approach to decolonisation at this stage of our nation’s journey of national development. We support full decolonisation now,” Golding told the Sunday Observer.

He recalled that last year September he wrote to Prime Minister Andrew Holness requesting to meet with him to see how the process could move forward, but that request was not granted.

“That is a counterproductive approach, given that these reforms will require bipartisan support in order to proceed…It is the Government, not the Opposition, that is delaying the process,” insisted the Opposition leader.

He stressed that it would be an anomaly for Jamaica to move away from the British monarch as our head of State but retain the British monarch’s court as our final court, and that anomaly would also perpetuate the existing system which has, for centuries, denied the vast majority of Jamaicans access to their final court.

“Because of the legislative history of this matter over the past two decades, we would only support the two things being done separately if the adoption of the CCJ as our final court is the first step of an agreed pathway to full decolonisation and Jamaica becoming a republic. However, our preference would be to pass the legislation for both things simultaneously, followed by the required referendum on the UK monarch being replaced as head of State by a Jamaican president,” said Golding.

He added that the Opposition also has concerns about the proposed manner of appointing the president, and the proposed changes to the composition and voting of the Senate. Additionally, he said there needs to be a consensus on term limits; fixed election dates; a procedure for the recall of delinquent MPs; a procedure for the impeachment of parliamentarians who bring their office into disrepute; a different arrangement for the appointment of the Speaker of the House to ensure greater independence and fairness; and the resumption of the convention whereby parliamentary committees are chaired by the Opposition.

“It will be important for there to be both public education and public consultations on these matters, and on any other constitutional reforms for which there is significant public support,” said Golding.

He further urged Jamaicans to put pressure on the Government to commence authentic dialogue with the Opposition as to a pathway for achieving full decolonisation.

Constitutional reform has been talked about for decades in Jamaica, across different political administrations.

Different committees have been established by both parties, with the most recent being the Constitutional Reform Committee established by the Andrew Holness-led Government in 2023.

World.title: JA celebrates!
World.content:
Fireworks display at Grand Gala celebrations inside the National Stadium..

For the annual week-long celebrations commemorating Jamaica’s ‘Emancipendence’, party-lovers and cultural enthusiasts have planned a calendar of activities unlike any other. From cultural showcases and gospel concerts to all-night parties and special holiday menus, Emancipendence 2026 has something for everyone.

Whether you’re looking to wave the black, green, and gold at a community event, dance until sunrise at a nightclub, or indulge in specially curated festive cuisine at your favourite restaurant, the island’s social calendar is packed with activities guaranteed to keep the celebratory spirit alive.

The festivities truly began with the naming of the winner of the 2026 Festival Song competition, and it continued in earnest on Saturday last with the grand coronation show for the 2026 Festival Queen, one of the season’s most cherished traditions. The event, which celebrates the intelligence, talent and cultural awareness of Jamaican women, has long been a staple of the Emancipendence calendar.

For those seeking spiritual inspiration, earlier on Saturday was the annual Come Alive Gospel Concert on the East Lawns at King’s House — an evening of worship, uplifting performances, and messages of hope.

Kingston’s nightlife scene is equally poised to come alive. Popular entertainment hot spot MECA has lined up several events throughout the holiday period, ensuring that revellers have no shortage of options to celebrate Jamaica’s rich culture and infectious energy.

According to MECA boss Michael Dawson, “Emancipendence is the time of year when the best of our culture and history is celebrated.” He shared that at MECA, the team feels “duty-bound to provide the nightlife to support that”. On their calendar is the weekly Dolly Sundays, An Evening With Tanya Stephens on Tuesday, and Nigy Boy in concert on Thursday.

Food lovers won’t be left out either, as Usain Bolt’s Tracks and Records (UBT&R) has rolled out a special Emancipendence menu, giving patrons the opportunity to savour local flavours and culinary favourites while embracing the festive spirit.

According to the Jizell Cowan, marketing manager at UBT&R, the menu is about “celebrating Jamaican culture, cuisine, and creativity”.

“Jamaicans love to ‘tun dem hand mek fashion’ in the kitchen, and this menu proves it,” she said. “We took our motto ‘Out of Many, One People’ and put it on a plate with fusion dishes like our Oxtail Boa Bus with an Asian twist, the Yaad Burrito with Hispanic flavour, and Curry Goat Pizza with an Italian touch.”

“It’s a delicious way for lovers of Jamaican cuisine to indulge and celebrate all month long this August. Plus it’s Rum Month and we are featuring Jamaican crafted rum like Appleton Estate Spanish Sherry,” she added.

Meanwhile, in Montego Bay, Dream Weekend party lovers are expected to continue celebrations. With activities having started on Thursday night, hundreds of party lovers have already descended on the second city eager to soak up the vibrant atmosphere that has become synonymous with the summer season.

But Emancipendence is about more than parties and late-night entertainment. It’s a season rooted in history — a celebration of the abolition of slavery in 1838 and Jamaica’s attainment of Independence in 1962. Every concert, every flag raised and every gathering serves as a reminder of the resilience, creativity, and pride that define the Jamaican people.

The celebrations will culminate on August 6 with the annual Grand Gala, the country’s premier Independence event. Slated for the National Stadium, the event will be filled with cultural performances, musical tributes, and dazzling fireworks. The spectacle is expected to bring thousands together in a fitting conclusion to a season dedicated to freedom and nationhood.

So whether you’re planning to sing, dance, pray, or simply bask in the festive atmosphere, one thing is certain: Jamaica is ready to celebrate.

World.title: Trump to restart Iran talks after scrapping planned strikes
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran would resume Monday, after scrapping a planned military strike over the weekend. Speaking on Sunday, the American leader also refused to set a deadline for reaching a broader deal with Tehran.

“They knew the extent of the attack because they saw it forming. Now what we’re doing is we’re talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon, and we’ll see,” said Trump, talking to reporters aboard Air Force One.

Asked whether he had imposed a deadline, the U.S. president responded: “Would I rather make a deal? I’m not looking to kill people because people die, a lot of people die, and we don’t want that.”

Trump’s remarks came on the heels of his early Sunday announcement on Truth Social that the U.S. was shelving a “massive attack,” after Iran and several Middle Eastern countries asked Washington to pause military action while negotiators worked toward an agreement. He said the framework under discussion included the “Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT” and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat, adding that Israel had also agreed to pause strikes.

So far, Tehran has not yet publicly confirmed it will take part in negotiations.

World.title: UEFA threatens Infantino, Joshua Kushner with legal action
World.content:
The FIFA chief’s plan to privatize part of the World Cup’s commercial operations sparked a major backlash in Brussels.

The governing body of European football, UEFA, has threatened legal action against FIFA President Gianni Infantino, venture capitalist Joshua Kushner — brother of U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner — and other individuals involved in the controversial plan to privatize a share of the World Cup’s commercial operations.

UEFA is “actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints” against Infantino, reads a letter sent to Infantino, seen by the Telegraph.

The move follows Infantino’s proposal to transfer FIFA’s commercial rights and tournament operations to a private entity firm — in partnership with Thrive Capital, Kushner’s venture capital company — allowing private investors to acquire a 20 percent stake.

World.title: What will Burnham do with the Budget?
World.content:
Andy Burnham has promised to transform Britain, but can he afford it?

This autumn, Chancellor John Healey will deliver the new government’s first Budget, so what might it include?

In the first episode of Sam and Anne’s summer box set, they sit down with Sky News’ economics editor Ed Conway to look at the spending choices facing the new prime minister.

How will the government tackle the cost of living? What do the bond markets make of Mr Burnham? And how much control does any chancellor really have when conflict in the Middle East and global events are shaping so much of Britain’s economy?

World.title: Ceuta triggers two days of EU emergency talks
World.content:
The crisis in the Spanish territory of Ceuta is adding fuel to Europe’s bitter debate over migration.

Following the arrival of more than 50,000 migrants in Ceuta in northern Africa last week, EU leaders ganged up on Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez over his migration policies. Although 48,300 migrants had returned to Morocco by late Friday, the backlash is ongoing. On Tuesday the EU is set to hold an urgent meeting of interior ministers to figure out next steps. Hosts Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart discuss the incident.

Next, European Ombudsman Teresa Anjinho warns that growing global crises can’t become an excuse for secrecy in the EU’s institutions. She says that more than a third of the complaints she receives are about transparency.

Plus: French President Emmanuel Macron’s team is looking for Saudi funding for a manga theme park near Paris.

World.title: Europe’s ETS revision is an opportunity to strengthen maritime competitiveness
World.content:
For Europe’s maritime sector—and beyond—the European Commission’s proposal to revise the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) goes in the right direction and reflects much of what Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA) has consistently called for: a framework in which carbon pricing supports, rather than holds back, the maritime transition, strengthens Europe’s industrial competitiveness and preserves connectivity, including for outermost regions. The starting point is an encouraging one.

Nikos Mertzanidis, executive director, Europe, Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA)

The proposal matters because it is about far more than carbon pricing. Not that the sector shies away from that: cruise lines already comply with the ETS, in addition to port dues, passenger charges, tonnage-based taxes and value-added tax (VAT). Unlike traditional taxation, the ETS is designed to drive decarbonization. Its revision matters because, by reinvesting a greater share of maritime ETS revenues in infrastructure—ports, shore-side electricity, alternative fuels, bunkering and other facilities—Europe can help the maritime industry maintain its global leadership while accelerating the energy transition. That leadership is not a matter of prestige. It is a matter of European prosperity, jobs, skills, competitiveness and industrial capacity across the continent.

The cruise industry alone generates an annual economic impact of €64.1 billion in Europe and supports 445,000 jobs. It is also one of Europe’s industrial success stories, combining world-leading shipbuilding, advanced engineering and maritime innovation with high-value tourism. Behind those figures lies a shipbuilding story that few industries can match: 98 percent of the global cruise orderbook is built in European shipyards, from Fincantieri in Italy to Chantiers de l’Atlantique in France and the Meyer yards in Germany and Finland. There is €62.2 billion committed to ships on order through 2037. This investment sustains a vast ecosystem of engineering firms, technology providers and thousands of suppliers, keeping in Europe the skills and industrial capacity that other regions of the world are actively trying to attract.

By reinvesting a greater share of maritime ETS revenues in infrastructure—ports, shore-side electricity, alternative fuels, bunkering and other facilities—Europe can help the maritime industry maintain its global leadership while accelerating the energy transition.

That is why it is important to be clear about cruise’s role in Europe. Cruise is a key part of the maritime industry: we build ships, move people between ports and across seas, and help drive innovation and investment through one of the most advanced supply chains in Europe. Cruise should therefore be understood first and foremost as part of Europe’s maritime industrial ecosystem, combining maritime transport, advanced manufacturing and tourism in a way few sectors do. It is governed by an extensive regulatory framework alongside the rest of international shipping while supporting one of Europe’s most innovative maritime value chains.

Via Shutterstock

Cruise represents just a small fraction of the global fleet—less than one percent of commercial vessels—but it is consistently at the forefront of maritime’s transformation in ways that benefit the broader maritime sector. Decarbonization is our north star, and our experience shows that it advances fastest when it travels hand in hand with innovation. Done well, decarbonization is not only an environmental objective but also a driver of industrial modernization and European competitiveness. This is why cruise matters to Europe’s maritime future: the industry is helping to turn decarbonization ambition into industrial progress—investing more than €44 billion since 2022 in new ships designed to meet or exceed Europe’s environmental regulations to improve performance and advance the maritime transition.

The cruise industry alone generates an annual economic impact of €64.1 billion in Europe and supports 445,000 jobs. It is also one of Europe’s industrial success stories, combining world-leading shipbuilding, advanced engineering and maritime innovation with high-value tourism.

More than half of the capacity on order today is capable of using liquefied natural gas (LNG), which can reduce CO2 emissions by up to 20 percent compared with conventional fuels. And while LNG is not the end-game solution, it does serve as an important bridge to lower-emissions fuels like renewable and synthetic methane as these types of fuels become available at scale. Today, 57 percent of cruise ships on order are designed with multi-fuel capability, meaning their engines will be able to run on low and zero greenhouse gas fuels, when available at scale. In addition, more than 60 percent of the global cruise fleet can already connect to shore-side electricity where ports are equipped, allowing ships to switch engines off at berth and reduce emissions by up to 98 percent. By 2028, close to 75 percent of capacity will be shore-power-ready.

The environmental transition is broader than carbon reduction alone. Across the global fleet, 225 ships—80 percent of the fleet and 84 percent of passenger capacity—are outfitted with advanced wastewater treatment systems, with more than a third capable of meeting stricter Baltic Sea Special Area discharge standards. More than 94 percent of the reporting fleet produces freshwater onboard, and approximately 60 percent can meet their full onboard consumption needs. Together, the cruise sector’s advancements in environmental technologies and practices help reduce emissions, support responsible operations and lessen pressure on local infrastructure in the destinations cruise ships visit.

Europe leads the world in cruise shipbuilding, maritime innovation and the deployment of technologies that can help decarbonize shipping.

Via CLIA

None of this happens in isolation from the places we serve. Cruise itineraries are planned up to three years in advance, which makes cruise one of the most predictable forms of tourism and allows ports, destinations and operators to manage visitor flows together. The economic footprint is tangible and local: when a ship provisions in port, a single day’s order of fresh produce alone can be worth some €150,000 to local suppliers, before counting fuel, services, excursions and the wider activity a call generates. And because cruise ships connect islands, outermost regions and remote coastal communities—often where alternative transport links are limited—cruise can extend the tourism season and spread benefits well beyond the traditional hotspots.

The road ahead, through the European Parliament, Council and trilogues, will be long, and we will walk it constructively together with our members and institutions at every stage. But the compass is set. Europe leads the world in cruise shipbuilding, maritime innovation and the deployment of technologies that can help decarbonize shipping. By preserving that leadership and reinvesting the sector’s ETS contribution into maritime infrastructure, fuels and facilities, the ETS will not merely price emissions—it will help build the ports, fuels and ships of the future, preserving the competitiveness and global leadership of Europe’s maritime industry for decades to come.
