World.title: Two men arrested after fake gun incident in Sydney's east
World.content:
Two men are in custody following an incident involving a fake gun at Sydney's Moore Park on Monday evening.

The police operation unfolded at the Entertainment Quarter about 4:45pm, with officers swarming the area following reports a person had a firearm.

In a statement, NSW Police said they found two men, one of which was allegedly carrying a firearm and wearing a bullet proof vest with an American flag on it.

The pair, aged 39 and 35, were arrested and a replica firearm, vest and badge were seized.

Several items were seized by police. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Both men were taken into custody and transported to Surry Hills Police Station.

Officers also confirmed the gun involved was fake and there was no ongoing threat to public safety.

Witness recounts 'really scary' incident

A woman eating out in the area with a friend recounted the "terrifying" ordeal.

"My friend saw out of the corner of his eye a man coming forward and we saw a gun on his chest," she said.

"But we were like, 'Is he wearing a costume, is it real?' It looked like a pistol.

"He went away and that's when my friend called the police because we didn't know where he was going and he could have a real gun."

Two men are in police custody. (ABC News)

The woman said that was when the pair called police to provide details, but the man came back.

"At that point the police were already on their way and we kind of got a closer look at him. He was actually right next to us outside the store," she said.

"That's when all of the police arrived and they got him on the ground and everything was fine.

"Obviously that's terrifying seeing a man with a gun. It was really scary ... I've never seen something like that happen in real life so it was terrifying."

One man driving past said about 15 to 20 police cars raced to the scene.

"It looked all pretty hectic. It looked insane," he said.

World.title: Hawks lock away coach Mitchell until 2030, Pies offer veteran another year
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Collingwood are keen for Jeremy Howe to play on next year.

The Selwood-like stat that has this young Blue on track for the Rising Star.

North Melbourne are acutely aware they’re the AFLW’s “hunted team” in 2026. Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell has inked three-year a contract extension that ties him to the Hawks until the end of 2030. Mitchell, who was already contracted for next season, has made no secret of his ambition to chase A-grade talent in the quest for a premiership after coaching the Hawks to consecutive finals series. Sam Mitchell is now contracted to Hawthorn until the end of 2030. Getty Images “Sam’s impact during his first five seasons as senior coach has been profound, and we’re delighted to extend his leadership through to 2030,” said Hawthorn chief executive Ash Klein.



“Having instilled elite standards whilst showing genuine care and connection with his players, Sam has cultivated an environment where every player can reach their full potential. Driven by his innate competitiveness, Sam’s ability to motivate, educate, and inspire our group is first class. “Additionally, Sam continues to demonstrate he is among the brightest minds in our game, with his forward-thinking and progressive coaching style setting our players up for sustainable success.” This masthead reported that Gold Coast free agent Ben King wants to play for the Hawks next year, while former Essendon skipper Zach Merrett is their next target.



Magpies offer Howe deal, uncertainty over others Jon Pierik Collingwood are keen for premiership defender Jeremy Howe to play on next year, as debate over the futures of Scott Pendlebury and Steele Sidebottom continue. An industry source confirmed on Monday that Howe had been offered a one-year extension by the Magpies, which would take his career into a 17th season. However, contract terms have yet to be rubber-stamped. The Magpies did not wish to comment when contacted by this masthead.



Playing on: Evergreen Pies star Jeremy Howe. AFL Photos Howe, 36, has played 287 games through his time at Melbourne and the Magpies, and is within sight of the 300-game milestone. He has undergone surgery on a broken left arm hurt during last Thursday’s loss to Geelong. A steel plate has been inserted, giving Howe hope of a return before the end of the home-and-away season. The ninth-placed Magpies are fighting for a wildcard berth, but have had their backline decimated by injury, for they are also without skipper Darcy Moore, Brayden Maynard and Harry Perryman, the latter straining a hamstring against the Cats. What now: What will Jeremy Howe be doing in 2027? AFL Photos



Howe has retained his high-flying athleticism even late in his career, while his ability to marshall the back six remains pivotal. There had been industry speculation Howe could have finished his career elsewhere and then moved into an assistant coaching role. A proud Tasmanian, he has been linked to joining the Tasmania Devils when they enter the league in 2028. While Howe’s 2027 plans appear clear, the Magpies have a major call to make on fellow veterans Sidebottom and Pendlebury. As reported by this masthead, the Magpies are expected to announce Sidebottom’s retirement before the season’s close, and are open to Pendlebury to either retire or seek to finish his playing days at another club and then be an assistant coach there. Pendlebury, set to turn 39 in January, is averaging 24 disposals per game this year, his highest return since 2019. He told this masthead last month he had yet to make a call on next year.



“I’m not sure about next year. My focus is still on this year, and performances like this give me belief that this group can do special things this year,” Pendlebury said.



The Selwood-like stat that has this young Blue on track for the Rising Star Jon Pierik Jagga Smith and Harry Dean have been central to rallying the Carlton faithful, the fans’ roar as visceral as it’s been in years when a Smith handball led to Dean’s first AFL goal at Marvel Stadium on Saturday night. Each is firmly in the running for the AFL Rising Star award, but Smith may have the edge. His elite form puts himon a par with a four-time premiership great for his offensive influence at this stage of his career. Happy days: Jagga Smith was nothing short of superb for the Blues against the Brisbane Lions. Getty Images



Smith, who sat out the 2025 campaign because of a knee reconstruction, has clocked up 129 score involvements, matching Geelong champion Joel Selwood for the most by a young player 20 games into his career, excluding mature-age recruits. He has overtaken Jesse Hogan (124 with Melbourne), Cyril Rioli (122 with Hawthorn) and Isaac Heeney (121 for the Swans) in powering to the top of the leaderboard with Selwood, whose influence on the Cats in 2007 was central to their premiership. Selwood was also named the Rising Star that year, edging Scott Pendlebury. Smith had arguably the most influential match of his young career against the Brisbane Lions, enjoying 29 possessions, including six clearances and two goals when pitted against a premiership-laden midfield, and was named the Robert Walls medallist. Joel Selwood when he won the Rising Star award in 2007. John Donegan This was the first time he had booted multiple goals in a game, taking his tally for the season to seven - the same number Selwood finished with all those years ago.



As Fox Footy analyst David King has noted, Smith makes good, quick decisions and is “prepared to bite off the risky kick”. His ability to find speed and dish off a snappy handball at a centre ball up was a highlight of his performance against the Lions, helping to ignite the Blues’ running game. Related Article Four Points

AFL 2026 ‘Clarko’ looks exasperated. It’s time for a hard conversation AFL great James Hird said the Oakleigh Chargers product had been integral to allowing Patrick Cripps and Sam Walsh to enjoy season-best form. “What I liked about Carlton, Jagga Smith, obviously playing well, Walsh and Cripps can actually do their job, they can do what they are best at,” Hird told Nine’s Footy Furnace. “That’s actually win the ball around the contest, give a good handball and let the other players on the outside [go to work]. They are not having to do it all.”



Hird’s comments are reinforced by more than 15 of Smith’s 26.4 touches per game being uncontested, with 11.5 handball receives. He leads the league in loose ball gets (7.1 per game). After such a commanding win over the Lions, Blues coach Josh Fraser, understandably, praised his entire youth movement. “We’ve got exciting youth, really exciting youth. They bring a youthful exuberance to the way they play. ‘Deany’ kicking that goal, you could see what that meant to him and those around him. Jagga has been very consistent for a while now,” Fraser said. Getting a move on: Patrick Cripps has been allowed to do what he does best, and that’s take charge at stoppages. Getty Images “Lachie Cowan doesn’t get spoken about a lot, but he’s a young player that is so important for us. Billy Wilson is growing his game, Cooper Lord has come in and is playing important roles. And there’s other guys that are performing at a high standard, so I’m really excited about the youth of the group.



“We know we’ve got more work in front of us, but what they’ve been able to bring has elevated our performance across the board. Those guys are as hungry as anyone to get better, the way they’re tipping into their game and investing in their game.” Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Bomber suffers concussion in friendly fire clash; Dees grind out win on Gold Coast; Tigers off the bottom Dean’s attention to detail has been extolled by fellow defender Jacob Weitering, describing the son of a gun as the “ultimate competitor” who has “some nastiness about him”. St Kilda coach Ross Lyon was a keen onlooker on Saturday night, and now must find a way to curb a midfield that has helped Fraser to a staggering 9-2 record as caretaker coach when the two teams meet in a finals-shaping blockbuster on Sunday night. Weitering is pushing for a recall from calf issues, and will look to strengthen his push when the Blues train on Wednesday.





‘The competition is coming after us.’ North Melbourne ready to remain the AFLW’s hunted Scott Spits Days after the AFLW’s best talent went from fierce rivals to loyal teammates for the historic Australia versus Ireland international match, the focus sharply turns to the biggest challenge in “the W”: finding a way to break North Melbourne’s stranglehold on the competition. The Kangaroos boast one of the best current records in Australian sport: a 27-match winning streak that has delivered back-to-back premierships. Due to the quirks of AFLW competition (shortened seasons that limit competition between clubs) and an early season draw against Geelong in 2024, it’s 32 months since the Darren Crocker-coached North Melbourne have experienced defeat. Selfie time: Carlton’s Abbie McKay gets the AFLW group photo organised. Getty Images



While AFLW season 11 will kick off on Sunday as part of a St Kilda versus Carlton double-header with the men’s competition, the Kangas will launch their premiership defence against Geelong on 15 August. But North Melbourne star Jasmine Garner, an AFLW stalwart who was part of the Australian team that beat the Irish by 50 points at North Sydney Oval on Saturday, is acutely aware that the team from Arden Street is in each of their opponent’s sights. “I think we’ve come into this pre-season with a mindset of ‘OK, how do we keep getting better’. Because the competition is coming after us, we know that,” Garner said on Monday. “We’re not shying away from it. “We just keep [focusing on] building our brand of footy. There’s little things that we’ve been trying to work on this pre-season, and we’ve had good success in our praccy games.”



Brisbane Lions captain Breanna Koenen says the Kangas have “a massive target on their back”. Koenen has had an up-close vantage point as the Roos ruled supreme in consecutive grand finals, both times easily having the Lions’ measure. “North have obviously been the standard for quite a long time now. What is their [consecutive wins] record now – 27 games?,” Koenen says. “There’s a massive target on their back but, bloody hell, it’s hard [trying to find a way to beat them]. “When you’re that good, I feel that every team almost circles you on the fixture, and they try and come out and play their best footy against you. “Tough, but pressure is a privilege I guess.”



St Kilda’s Serene Watson and Carlton’s Abbie McKay. AFL Photos Last year’s grand final margin blew out to 50 points as the ruthless Roos put an exclamation mark on two seasons of dominance. Naturally Koenen has watched a replay of the game. It just didn’t happen immediately. “You’d be crazy not to,” she says. “You’ve just got to use that as a learning experience, at the end of the day.” Adelaide star Ebony Marinoff, another competition stalwart, says taming the rampant Roos is the priority. “You’ve just got to keep striving,” the 28-year-old says.



“At the end of the day you have to be able to respect and honour what North Melbourne has been able to do. “I’m a competitor but at the end of the day when someone is successful … there’s so much respect there for what you’ve been able to do. “And having been coached under Crocs [North Melbourne coach Darren Crocker, who also led the Australian coaching contingent against Ireland] for the last few days, you can understand why he’s so successful. His story-telling was incredible, just the way that he expressed himself and got around …. the whole of the group,” she said. “They’re very lucky to have him at the helm. “[While] I think anyone can be beaten, it’s going to be hard to stop them.



“They have so much depth amongst their list, but I think for all of us you’ve just got to keep striving.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Misdirected or misleading? Health boss in hot water over estimates show
World.content:
Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: the estimates comments which struck a nerve (or got a laugh), police union spills tea on government talks, and a brewing mystery in the Tower of Power. The joy that is budget estimates delivered no shortage of the usual for senior unelected officials: government protection, bizarre opposition gotcha efforts, and the occasional eye-opening answer. But one director-general’s doozy seems to have struck a nerve – and frustrated someone in their orbit enough to pick up the phone to pose the question: did David Rosengren mislead his hearing? Queensland Health director-general David Rosengren at Tuesday’s estimates hearing. Queensland parliament We ran the ruler last week over the Queensland Health chief’s explanation for having three hospital and health service boards without a legally required First Nations director.



In case you missed that, Rosengren said the vacancies were the “unscheduled” result of resignations “subsequent to” the process of the March HHS board overhaul. The facts suggest otherwise. At Metro North (the state’s largest HHS) and Metro South (no.2, with the largest Indigenous population), three directors were either handed midterm marching orders or gave earlier notice. Up on the Sunshine Coast, Circus has learned that not only did Bundjalung man Terry Bell not resign after the recent recruitment round, but that he had reapplied for the board. Twice! It’s all been enough to drive one board insider, who we’ve granted anonymity to get around the fact they’re unauthorised to speak publicly, to get us on the blower and call the situation out.



They confirmed the detail about Bell’s efforts to remain on the board, and said it appeared Rosengren had “misled the estimates committee”, suggesting he should explain or apologise. Related Article Public service LNP-sponsor data centre firm taps ex-premier to join major meetings Not a minor thing, given parliamentary rules leave any deliberate misleading of proceedings by MPs open to a contempt finding. Let alone the maximum seven-year penalty for anyone else giving false evidence to parliament under the Criminal Code. Circus is, of course, not suggesting Rosengren is guilty of any such thing. Only that his evidence did not align with the facts as we understand them, and he has to date given no explanation as to why. In our generosity, we’d also posit that he was perhaps misinformed by three separate HHS boards.



For their part, we’ve sung out to the four former directors and have either been unable to reach them or found them politely declining to speak about both their departures or Rosengren’s remarks. We also put the insider’s assessment to Rosengren via the Queensland Health media team on Monday, along with a nudge for the still unanswered questions from last week. “To protect the privacy of individual applicants and comply with confidentiality obligations, Queensland Health is not able to provide specific details regarding the board recruitment process,” came the week-in-the-making response from a department spokesperson. For what it’s worth, Health Minister Tim Nicholls’ office reckons it’s all a matter for the bureaucrats – a bit rich given the ultimate appointment decisions are ones for him. While Circus is loath to share official backgrounding, such spin work in this case has sought to explain the “unscheduled” labelling of the gaps, but not the resignation element. Read into that what you will.



And the estimates comedy award goes too... Elsewhere across the 70 hours and 15 minutes of hearings over nine days, there were at last a few successful efforts to break the stuffy (or petty) nature of proceedings with some humour. But it was hard to look past the deadpanned delivery of Department of Sport, Racing and Olympic and Paralympic Games director-general Andrew Hopper as the gold standard. Department of Sport, Racing and Olympic and Paralympic Games director-general (and funny guy) Andrew Hopper. Queensland Parliament One pressure-release came after two minutes of bickering sparked by a question from Kurwongbah Labor MP Shane King about 2025-26 advertising campaigns.



This topic was the trigger for countless points of order by government MPs across the fortnight, a campaign led by Leader of the House Dr Christian Rowan. Related Article Perspective

Queensland government Five key questions that went unanswered in the first week of Qld’s scrutiny show King ultimately labelled Rowan’s efforts in this circumstance “frivolous”, which the member for Moggill took as personally offensive and had withdrawn. Speaker Pat Weir managed to dam the duelling interruptions long enough to give the call to Hopper. “My apologies, member, there was a bit going on there. Could you please repeat the question,” the department head quipped with the slightest hint of a smirk. Cue bipartisan laughter.



For contrast, Hopper’s earlier request for clarification from Labor’s opposition sports spokesperson Glenn Butcher during a line of questioning about the delayed government sport strategy was among the most cutting. Hopper: “Just to clarify, you are asking if there was money allocated in 2025-26 for a strategy that has been released today. I will take a moment for that.” After turning to speak to a colleague for all of 10 seconds, he continued: “Member, obviously with the release of the strategy in the financial year 2026-27, that is where the money is allocated.” No laughter from the chamber at that zinger. What government and police chief told union crowd



Among all the estimates fun, it would be excusable if we missed the release of the Winter 2026 edition of the Queensland Police Union Journal. But thanks to a reminder from some eagle-eyed members of the tent, we were able to catch up on all the juicy goss from the annual coppers’ collective council meeting back in May. Inside were speeches (and Q&A sessions) from acting Commissioner Brett Pointing, Premier David Crisafulli and Police Minister Dan Purdie, dutifully transcribed and published in full. And what did the political leaders and top brass have to tell union president Shane Prior’s troops? A bit of that has already been aired by our Campbell Street comrades, including approval from Crisafulli to collecting more DNA from youth offenders and supporting changes to pursuit laws.



Beyond that, Pointing also said cabinet had asked him to “come back with a model that would work better with the troops” on controversial instant domestic violence orders. Dubbed police protection directions, and earlier decried by Prior as too onerous for use in most cases, Pointing conceded the powers had not “been as effective as we had all hoped it would be”. Then police minister Bill Byrne and Deputy Commissioner Brett Pointing in 2017. Amy Mitchell-Whittington “Whilst that is still cabinet in confidence, the model that we put up, if we get it through, I think will make a huge difference,” Pointing said. Another comment from the top brass that caught Circus’ eye was the fact, in his words, that “hardly a day goes by that Shane doesn’t ring”, particularly with about watchhouse and fleet concerns.



Despite all the backslapping, some more pointed elements of the gathering were captured in the questions from delegates and elsewhere in the journal. With the government spruiking of record spending in key frontline workforces, Prior’s opening comments describe the Crisafulli LNP’s 2026-27 budget as a “pretty bland affair … a bit like reheating Monday night’s dinner on Wednesday”. Regardless, Circus imagines Crisafulli and Co will be invited back – and show up – next year. Cold water poured on brewing mystery at 1WS With all the talk of stationery supplies being slashed as part of the Crisafulli government’s bid to find $500 million in public service savings, the case of the diminishing tea bag stock in One William Street has invoked fears for many.



Circus spies were quick to raise the alarm after tea bags, milk and sugar satchels ran dry in recent weeks, with staff fearing the austerity measures had come for the much-loved cuppa. The government insists the future of the smoko brew is safe, but how do they explain the missing bags and single-serve sweeteners? Public servants get access to automatic coffee machines for a small fee inside the Tower of Power, with the coins amassed through the machines used to stock tea stations. iStock The empty kitchens were caused by end-of-life coffee machines being replaced, Circus was told. You see, public servants get access to automatic coffee machines for a small fee inside the Tower of Power, with the coins amassed through the machines used to stock tea stations. But the older machines, which only accept coins, have been pulled from the building to make way for newer models which allow electronic payments.



Meanwhile, there’s no change floating around to pay for the depleted stock of tea, milk and sugar. As a tea-and-coffee-loving column on the side of our hard-working public servants, Circus pressed the relevant minister on the issue, Public Works Minister Sam O’Connor, whose spokeswoman sought to ease concerns. “Despite the brewing speculation, there is no change to the tea and coffee arrangements for staff at 1 William Street,” she said in response to questions. Thank goodness. Now, time to put the kettle on. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email us on m.dennien@nine.com.au or james.hall@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. World.title: We went to Panda Mart’s first Queensland store so you don’t have to
World.content:
The Queensland launch of discounted retail chain Panda Mart sparked a frenzy of shoppers, with thousands descending on the store in Brisbane’s south. The chain, described as “Temu in real life”, stocks everything from cosmetics and toys to homewares, furniture, sporting goods, outdoor gear and more. Panda Mart in Rocklea has 18 checkout counters, all of which had a line on Monday afternoon. A staff member, not authorised to speak publicly and who asked not to be named, said he served at least 1000 customers at his counter alone over the weekend.



“18 counters and 1000 people through each,” he said. “More than 1000 I reckon, I’m not sure though. It’s just a lot of people. On Saturday, Sunday it’s more. People coming in every two minutes. Panda Mart has officially opened at Rocklea in Brisbane’s south. Dominique Tassell “Every time you look over there, it’s just people, it never settles down.” The worker estimated there were 60 to 70 per cent more people on Saturday and Sunday than on Monday.



Just after midday on Monday, limited parking had forced customers to drive off-road and on the sidewalk before piling into the store located at the old Bunnings site. Cars were parked in every available space on the lawns – up on the curbs, and on every side street for at least three blocks. By 2pm, a line had formed at the door with entry staggered by staff to a few at a time. Shelves were bare for some items, with the most popular products being snacks, makeup, and furniture. Shoppers who visited the store over the weekend shared footage online of messy aisles, particularly in the rug section of the store.



Rugs were strewn across the floor in piles, blocking the aisles so no one could walk through. Related Article Retail We shop at ‘Temu in real life’. Are the products safe? Panda Mart first launched in South Africa in 2010, and launched in Victoria last year. Crowds were so large at the Cranbourne store opening in Melbourne’s outskirts that police had to be called. Police were not required at the Rocklea store during its soft opening weekend. The chain’s Victorian stores were ordered to stop trading for 72 hours by Consumer Affairs Victoria last December, while allegedly unsafe goods were seized.



In January, 147 criminal charges were laid by the consumer watchdog against Panda Mart Cranbourne for selling unsafe products. Panda Mart Cranbourne also faces 130 charges over allegedly unsafe lamps and other electrical products after scrutiny from Energy Safe Victoria. Items seized from the Victorian stores include toys and baby rattles with button batteries, which can kill or seriously injure a child if swallowed. In March, further items were seized including flammable candleholders banned in Australia due to burns and fire risks. World.title: ‘Forgotten victim’ in Keli Lane saga speaks out
World.content:
The adult daughter of convicted killer Keli Lane says she is a forgotten victim of her mother’s ongoing detention and has urged her release on parole with more than two years remaining on her sentence.

“I am a forgotten victim in this situation,” the now 25-year-old daughter wrote in a letter to authorities, provided to Nine’s A Current Affair program.

Convicted killer Keli Lane pictured with her daughter, who now aged 25, is urging for her mother’s release on parole. A Current Affair

“My hope is simple: that my mum can come home and that I can spend meaningful time with her, that is all I wish for.”

She recalled being dropped at school by her mother when she was nine years old, the last time she saw her before Lane was taken into custody after being convicted of the 1996 murder of her baby daughter Tegan.

World.content:

Warning: Graphic content Washington: US Republican senator Bernie Moreno broke his silence on Sunday (Washington time) about a years-long family drama involving domestic abuse allegations against his former son-in-law, Republican congressman Max Miller, saying in an emotional statement that Miller was not fit to hold public office. Moreno, saying the dispute had put his family through “pure hell”, scathingly denounced Miller, whose ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused him of abusing her and their two-year-old daughter. Congressman Max Miller of Ohio has denied the accusations and vowed that he is “not getting out of this race”. Bloomberg “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” Bernie Moreno wrote in a post on the social platform X. He added: “I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter.”



He continued: “He should not serve in the House of Representatives. I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake. I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does.” Related Article Analysis

US election Trump lays the groundwork for emergency declaration ahead of midterms The Ohio senator issued his statement in reaction to an earlier, defiant livestream on Sunday by Miller, who is seeking re-election in Ohio’s 7th Congressional District. Miller denied the accusations and vowed that he was “not getting out of this race”. Miller is running in a tight race in what had been a safe seat for Republicans before the allegations became public. Moreno’s statement, his first on the issue, seems likely to further damage Miller’s campaign, a source of concern for Republicans nationally even as they have largely maintained public silence. The wrenching public back-and-forth came just three days before the deadline for Republicans to replace Miller on the ballot – or risk locking him in as the GOP nominee for a seat that has become competitive in large part because of the allegations against him. Miller appears to be just 1 percentage point ahead of his Democratic challenger, according to internal polling research by Democrats, in a district that US President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024.



Until now, Republicans across the board have chosen not to denounce Miller or call for his resignation, dismissing the charges against him as mere “allegations”. It was not clear on Sunday how Moreno’s weighing in would shift the response from other Republicans. In a roughly 20-minute livestream, Miller categorically denied all the accusations that Emily Moreno has levelled at him in court. He also claimed that she had “significant mental health challenges”, without offering any evidence. Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio says the dispute has put his family through “pure hell”. AP Photo/Allison Robbert Miller said he had never scalded Moreno’s chest and stomach by throwing hot water from a skillet at her body, as she has accused him, dismissing the incident as “horseplay in our kitchen” with water that was not boiling. He also denied her accusation that he held a gun to her head, and he vehemently rejected her charge that he had fractured their daughter’s collarbone and bruised her shoulder.



Miller, a former staff member for Trump, blamed his daughter’s injuries on two daycare workers. Related Article US election Can a left-wing Muslim win the Midwest? Or are Democrats about to make a big mistake “If these accusations were true, I would be in jail,” Miller said, seated in his kitchen and reading haltingly from a script. He contended that the credibility of her assertions was undermined by the fact that he still retains joint custody after years of court battles. In his livestream, Miller repeatedly pointed to examples of what he claimed were friendly overtures from Moreno as proof that she was fabricating the claims of abuse. “If I had assaulted her, would she have offered to cook me dinner six days later?” he asked. Moreno is seeking to end their shared parenting agreement. The issue is expected to go to court on November 5. Last week, Moreno filed a restraining order against Miller, claiming he had harassed and threatened her lawyers.



Immediately after his livestream, Miller made public a trove of recordings, text message exchanges and court documents that he said would prove his innocence. A lawyer for Moreno did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump’s entered a new phase: the unmaking of his presidency Bruce Wolpe Senior fellow at the US Studies Centre and former political staffer Amid broad silence from Republicans, Democrats have called for a House ethics committee investigation into the allegations against Miller. Speaker Mike Johnson has said only that there is an ethics process for handling such accusations. He did not respond to a request for comment on Sunday. Republican congressman Jim Jordan, also from Ohio, defended Miller in a recent interview. “This is a family matter. I know Max is a good man,” he told CNN. “I hope he wins re-election.” Behind the scenes, however, Republicans in Trump’s orbit have said they are alarmed by Miller’s decision to go on the offensive against Moreno and are concerned about his re-election campaign.



Miller, however, expressed deep confidence on Sunday that he would be back in Congress next year. “This election to me is about my family and about our daughter and keeping our values here and holding the media and other individuals accountable,” he said. Emily Moreno is not the first woman to level domestic abuse allegations against Miller. In her memoir, Stephanie Grisham, a former White House press secretary, wrote that she dated someone in the administration who was physically abusive. She later acknowledged that she had been referring to Miller. If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: ‘Can’t keep kids safe’: Inherent risks in market-driven childcare
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaEducation ‘Can’t keep kids safe’: Inherent risks in market-driven childcare Nicole Precel August 3, 2026 — 7:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Childcare worker Sherry used to wake up every morning unsure of how to keep the 11 children in her care safe. “It hurts me as a teacher that you can’t keep the children in your care safe,” she said. “It’s stressful and overwhelming.” Lauren Treweek with sons Gus, 1, who goes to daycare, and Xavier, 3, who goes to kinder. Joe Armao The 30-year-old, who asked not to use her surname to speak openly, said challenging behaviours, a one-to-11 ratio and little support from management made it an impossible job and inherently risky. A report from Victoria University’s Mitchell Institute found the push to expand childcare had created workforce churn, provider turnover and growing risk.



Since 2013, 40.7 per cent of for-profit centres have changed operators, some as many as five times, the report shows. Analysis of the workforce found the median hourly wage for educators is akin to cleaners – $34.30, compared with $62 for schoolteachers. It is below the median hourly wage of $42.40. The most recent data from the Australian Taxation Office (2022/2023) shows 52 per cent of jobs in the childcare sector were held for less than a year. To compound the lack of continuity, large for-profit private providers (with more than 25 centres) were more than three times as likely to have an enforcement action recorded than centres run by not-for-profit or community providers.



Mitchell Institute director Professor Peter Hurley said using markets to boost childcare places while keeping prices down had come at a cost. “These approaches bake-in the deficiencies of low pay and high turnover and put enormous strain on the sector. They end up rewarding those providers who can produce an hour of care in the cheapest way possible while meeting the minimum standards,” he said. Lauren Treweek with her sons, Xavier, 3, and Gus, 1. Joe Armao Childcare centres receive childcare subsidy payments from the federal government ($16.9 billion in 2025-26) on behalf of families to deliver reduced-cost services. Closures and new centres are driven by the market. Hurley said the report, The price of a place: Instability, risk and the hidden cost of Australia’s early childhood education and care system, showed that the market had reduced barriers for operators to easily open or close centres.



“[Providers] can trial the market, and if it doesn’t work, they can leave,” he said. Mitchell Institute director Peter Hurley. Ruby Alexander. “That can work with something like an airline industry. When it comes to children, they’re extremely vulnerable. One of the things that really struck me with these horrible cases that’s been going on is just how many places they’ve worked,” he said. “That’s prompted us to look at this. The shorter nature of the employment and educators.” Major changes have been introduced since the childcare sector was plunged into crisis in July last year when horrific allegations of child sex abuse surfaced across Australia.



In Melbourne, accused childcare rapist Joshua Dale Brown is facing more than 100 charges, including sexually penetrating multiple children he was employed to care for. In Sydney, daycare worker Hamish Tait, 35, is facing more than 320 charges over his alleged abuse of more than 150 children. There’s since been a Victorian parliamentary inquiry, a shift in the Working With Children Check, tightening of market entry requirements, and the ability to suspend or cancel subsidy payments for serious breaches. The Front Project chief executive officer, Caroline Croser-Barlow, said recent measures to improve quality, such as stripping centres of the childcare subsidy for ongoing breaches, and worker-retention payments, had produced improvements. “Do I think we’ve done enough? Absolutely not.” The worst operators were those seeking to flip centres and profit, she said.



The amount of childcare places has almost doubled since 2013, from about 400,000 to about 730,000 - almost entirely by private for-profit providers who account for 74 per cent of long daycare places, the research shows. The Parenthood’s Georgie Dent said early education should be funded more like schools, as core public infrastructure, not a market to be left to its own devices. “That means funding that reflects the actual cost of delivering high-quality education and care: fair wages, stable staffing, professional development and safe facilities,” she said.



Mother-of-three Lauren Treweek said for parents, long daycare continued to be “unbelievably and astronomically expensive” amid “quite honestly terrifying stories”. “It seems like every time you get a break, in terms of the rebate being changed, the private centres just end up putting their fees up, or to be honest, centres in general,” she said. Treweek tried to get two of her children into the same childcare centre but couldn’t, so now has to do three separate drop-offs: one-year-old Gus at long daycare, Xavier, 3, to kindergarten, and Sienna, 5, to school. She said the short tenure of educators was concerning, as was a lack of transparency from operators. “How can you build trust in educators when they’re not even at the centre for a year, or the minute you drop your child off, you’re hoping for this great relationship, as they have with your family, and then, you know, six to 12 months later, they’re not there?” she said.



“I think the visibility that parents are being provided with is terrible. It’s shocking,” she said. Minister for Early Childhood Education Jess Walsh said the government was consulting on a national early education and care commission, which could help guide a path towards universal early childhood education and care, address undersupply and oversupply, and build a stronger system. Education ministers are due to meet to discuss its development in October. She said a 15 per cent pay rise for educators was stabilising the workforce, and states and territories were investing about half-a-billion dollars to support a package of reforms to lift safety and standards across the sector.



Hurley said it wasn’t for-profit centres that were the issue, but the childcare model itself, which required more research into alternatives. Childcare worker Sherry has moved to a sessional kindergarten. “It’s different. It’s not-for-profit, so I feel like the service is actually putting effort into supporting children,” she said. “Every service will say it’s children-centred, but in practice, it’s not. It’s profit-centred. Editor's pick Exclusive

Domestic violence WA watchdog probes police interactions with Virginia Giuffre



“We put children at risk. We put educators at risk as well.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Shocking video of patient assaulting nurse prompts union call for safer conditions
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Health Shocking video of patient assaulting nurse prompts union call for safer conditions Dominique Tassell August 3, 2026 — 7:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Footage of a registered nurse being attacked by a patient in the foyer of the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital in 2024 has gone viral, prompting the nurses union to call for safer working conditions. Daniel Nelson shared a video of the incident to his Facebook late last week, saying: “This is what many people never see.” Nelson was working in the RBWH Emergency Department in October 2024 when the incident occurred at 2am. “I was a victim of assault by an intoxicated patient in an area where there were no visibility from staff or security,” he said.



“He’d been spitting on the floor, abusing staff and generally behaving like an absolute grub. “[He] was asked to leave, I opted to escort him out and grab a cheeky coffee from the coffee van parked out front whilst I was out there. In a stroke of genius he decided he wanted a cuddle.” In the footage, the patient and Nelson almost make it out the doors of the hospital when the patient turns and throws his belongings at the nurse before physically attacking him. Daniel Nelson was working in the RBWH Emergency Department in October 2024 when the incident occurred at 2am. Facebook Nelson wrestles the patient to the floor, pinning him to the ground and restraining him until help arrives almost a full minute later.



“Safe to say... it didn’t work out the way he expected,” Nelson said. “I don’t think he anticipated the nurse having an obsession with jiu jitsu for over 10 years.” No level of violence against nurses, midwives and all health workers is acceptable, Queensland Nurses and Midwives’ Union Secretary Sarah Beaman said. “QNMU is deeply concerned about any incident that threatens the safety of nurses, other health professionals and patients,” Beaman said. Daniel Nelson wrestled the patient to the floor, pinning him to the ground and restraining him until help arrived almost a full minute later. Facebook “With national figures recently released by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare showing assault in the workplace has now climbed from the fourth to the second leading cause of hospitalisations for injuries among healthcare workers, we reiterate more needs to be done to protect our nurses.



“Nurses and midwives should not have to defend themselves from violent behaviour in the workplace.” While staff receive occupational violence prevention training, QNMU called for employers to do more to ensure there are safe working conditions. “We expect employers to do more to ensure when behaviour does escalate there are de-escalation measures in place that do not rely on nurses and midwives having to use reasonable force to protect themselves from harm,” Beaman said. “Occupational violence is at alarming levels, and this is not new news. We need urgent action by employers to protect nurses and midwives from further harm. “We call on employers to provide additional security measures and to strengthen workplace safety in all health care settings.”



Related Article Hospitals ‘Bashed, stabbed and spat at’: Violence in public hospitals on the rise The viral video coincides with the state government celebrating 10,000 new health workers in just under two years. Of these workers, 7200 are frontline doctors, nurses and allied health workers. The LNP previously pledged to deliver an additional 46,000 health workers by 2032. Premier David Crisafulli said the government is working to rebuild the state’s frontline.



“We made a promise to rebuild the health frontline, and with more than 10,000 frontline workers already delivered, that’s exactly what we’re doing,” he said. “We will continue to reduce ramping and stabilise the elective surgery waitlist by delivering more hospital beds and building the frontline workforce to ensure Queenslanders can access the health services when and where they need them.” Health Minister Tim Nicholls said employing more health professionals is just one part of the solution. “We will be doing all we can to attract and retain doctors, nurses, midwives, ambulance officers, allied health workers and other health workers to Queensland Health, especially to the areas they are needed most,” Nicholls said. World.title: Hawks lock away coach Mitchell until 2030, Pies offer veteran another year
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Collingwood are keen for Jeremy Howe to play on next year.

The Selwood-like stat that has this young Blue on track for the Rising Star.

North Melbourne are acutely aware they’re the AFLW’s “hunted team” in 2026. Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell has inked three-year a contract extension that ties him to the Hawks until the end of 2030. Mitchell, who was already contracted for next season, has made no secret of his ambition to chase A-grade talent in the quest for a premiership after coaching the Hawks to consecutive finals series. Sam Mitchell is now contracted to Hawthorn until the end of 2030. Getty Images “Sam’s impact during his first five seasons as senior coach has been profound, and we’re delighted to extend his leadership through to 2030,” said Hawthorn chief executive Ash Klein.



“Having instilled elite standards whilst showing genuine care and connection with his players, Sam has cultivated an environment where every player can reach their full potential. Driven by his innate competitiveness, Sam’s ability to motivate, educate, and inspire our group is first class. “Additionally, Sam continues to demonstrate he is among the brightest minds in our game, with his forward-thinking and progressive coaching style setting our players up for sustainable success.” This masthead reported that Gold Coast free agent Ben King wants to play for the Hawks next year, while former Essendon skipper Zach Merrett is their next target.



Magpies offer Howe deal, uncertainty over others Jon Pierik Collingwood are keen for premiership defender Jeremy Howe to play on next year, as debate over the futures of Scott Pendlebury and Steele Sidebottom continue. An industry source confirmed on Monday that Howe had been offered a one-year extension by the Magpies, which would take his career into a 17th season. However, contract terms have yet to be rubber-stamped. The Magpies did not wish to comment when contacted by this masthead.



Playing on: Evergreen Pies star Jeremy Howe. AFL Photos Howe, 36, has played 287 games through his time at Melbourne and the Magpies, and is within sight of the 300-game milestone. He has undergone surgery on a broken left arm hurt during last Thursday’s loss to Geelong. A steel plate has been inserted, giving Howe hope of a return before the end of the home-and-away season. The ninth-placed Magpies are fighting for a wildcard berth, but have had their backline decimated by injury, for they are also without skipper Darcy Moore, Brayden Maynard and Harry Perryman, the latter straining a hamstring against the Cats. What now: What will Jeremy Howe be doing in 2027? AFL Photos



Howe has retained his high-flying athleticism even late in his career, while his ability to marshall the back six remains pivotal. There had been industry speculation Howe could have finished his career elsewhere and then moved into an assistant coaching role. A proud Tasmanian, he has been linked to joining the Tasmania Devils when they enter the league in 2028. While Howe’s 2027 plans appear clear, the Magpies have a major call to make on fellow veterans Sidebottom and Pendlebury. As reported by this masthead, the Magpies are expected to announce Sidebottom’s retirement before the season’s close, and are open to Pendlebury to either retire or seek to finish his playing days at another club and then be an assistant coach there. Pendlebury, set to turn 39 in January, is averaging 24 disposals per game this year, his highest return since 2019. He told this masthead last month he had yet to make a call on next year.



“I’m not sure about next year. My focus is still on this year, and performances like this give me belief that this group can do special things this year,” Pendlebury said.



The Selwood-like stat that has this young Blue on track for the Rising Star Jon Pierik Jagga Smith and Harry Dean have been central to rallying the Carlton faithful, the fans’ roar as visceral as it’s been in years when a Smith handball led to Dean’s first AFL goal at Marvel Stadium on Saturday night. Each is firmly in the running for the AFL Rising Star award, but Smith may have the edge. His elite form puts himon a par with a four-time premiership great for his offensive influence at this stage of his career. Happy days: Jagga Smith was nothing short of superb for the Blues against the Brisbane Lions. Getty Images



Smith, who sat out the 2025 campaign because of a knee reconstruction, has clocked up 129 score involvements, matching Geelong champion Joel Selwood for the most by a young player 20 games into his career, excluding mature-age recruits. He has overtaken Jesse Hogan (124 with Melbourne), Cyril Rioli (122 with Hawthorn) and Isaac Heeney (121 for the Swans) in powering to the top of the leaderboard with Selwood, whose influence on the Cats in 2007 was central to their premiership. Selwood was also named the Rising Star that year, edging Scott Pendlebury. Smith had arguably the most influential match of his young career against the Brisbane Lions, enjoying 29 possessions, including six clearances and two goals when pitted against a premiership-laden midfield, and was named the Robert Walls medallist. Joel Selwood when he won the Rising Star award in 2007. John Donegan This was the first time he had booted multiple goals in a game, taking his tally for the season to seven - the same number Selwood finished with all those years ago.



As Fox Footy analyst David King has noted, Smith makes good, quick decisions and is “prepared to bite off the risky kick”. His ability to find speed and dish off a snappy handball at a centre ball up was a highlight of his performance against the Lions, helping to ignite the Blues’ running game. Related Article Four Points

AFL 2026 ‘Clarko’ looks exasperated. It’s time for a hard conversation AFL great James Hird said the Oakleigh Chargers product had been integral to allowing Patrick Cripps and Sam Walsh to enjoy season-best form. “What I liked about Carlton, Jagga Smith, obviously playing well, Walsh and Cripps can actually do their job, they can do what they are best at,” Hird told Nine’s Footy Furnace. “That’s actually win the ball around the contest, give a good handball and let the other players on the outside [go to work]. They are not having to do it all.”



Hird’s comments are reinforced by more than 15 of Smith’s 26.4 touches per game being uncontested, with 11.5 handball receives. He leads the league in loose ball gets (7.1 per game). After such a commanding win over the Lions, Blues coach Josh Fraser, understandably, praised his entire youth movement. “We’ve got exciting youth, really exciting youth. They bring a youthful exuberance to the way they play. ‘Deany’ kicking that goal, you could see what that meant to him and those around him. Jagga has been very consistent for a while now,” Fraser said. Getting a move on: Patrick Cripps has been allowed to do what he does best, and that’s take charge at stoppages. Getty Images “Lachie Cowan doesn’t get spoken about a lot, but he’s a young player that is so important for us. Billy Wilson is growing his game, Cooper Lord has come in and is playing important roles. And there’s other guys that are performing at a high standard, so I’m really excited about the youth of the group.



“We know we’ve got more work in front of us, but what they’ve been able to bring has elevated our performance across the board. Those guys are as hungry as anyone to get better, the way they’re tipping into their game and investing in their game.” Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Bomber suffers concussion in friendly fire clash; Dees grind out win on Gold Coast; Tigers off the bottom Dean’s attention to detail has been extolled by fellow defender Jacob Weitering, describing the son of a gun as the “ultimate competitor” who has “some nastiness about him”. St Kilda coach Ross Lyon was a keen onlooker on Saturday night, and now must find a way to curb a midfield that has helped Fraser to a staggering 9-2 record as caretaker coach when the two teams meet in a finals-shaping blockbuster on Sunday night. Weitering is pushing for a recall from calf issues, and will look to strengthen his push when the Blues train on Wednesday.





‘The competition is coming after us.’ North Melbourne ready to remain the AFLW’s hunted Scott Spits Days after the AFLW’s best talent went from fierce rivals to loyal teammates for the historic Australia versus Ireland international match, the focus sharply turns to the biggest challenge in “the W”: finding a way to break North Melbourne’s stranglehold on the competition. The Kangaroos boast one of the best current records in Australian sport: a 27-match winning streak that has delivered back-to-back premierships. Due to the quirks of AFLW competition (shortened seasons that limit competition between clubs) and an early season draw against Geelong in 2024, it’s 32 months since the Darren Crocker-coached North Melbourne have experienced defeat. Selfie time: Carlton’s Abbie McKay gets the AFLW group photo organised. Getty Images



While AFLW season 11 will kick off on Sunday as part of a St Kilda versus Carlton double-header with the men’s competition, the Kangas will launch their premiership defence against Geelong on 15 August. But North Melbourne star Jasmine Garner, an AFLW stalwart who was part of the Australian team that beat the Irish by 50 points at North Sydney Oval on Saturday, is acutely aware that the team from Arden Street is in each of their opponent’s sights. “I think we’ve come into this pre-season with a mindset of ‘OK, how do we keep getting better’. Because the competition is coming after us, we know that,” Garner said on Monday. “We’re not shying away from it. “We just keep [focusing on] building our brand of footy. There’s little things that we’ve been trying to work on this pre-season, and we’ve had good success in our praccy games.”



Brisbane Lions captain Breanna Koenen says the Kangas have “a massive target on their back”. Koenen has had an up-close vantage point as the Roos ruled supreme in consecutive grand finals, both times easily having the Lions’ measure. “North have obviously been the standard for quite a long time now. What is their [consecutive wins] record now – 27 games?,” Koenen says. “There’s a massive target on their back but, bloody hell, it’s hard [trying to find a way to beat them]. “When you’re that good, I feel that every team almost circles you on the fixture, and they try and come out and play their best footy against you. “Tough, but pressure is a privilege I guess.”



St Kilda’s Serene Watson and Carlton’s Abbie McKay. AFL Photos Last year’s grand final margin blew out to 50 points as the ruthless Roos put an exclamation mark on two seasons of dominance. Naturally Koenen has watched a replay of the game. It just didn’t happen immediately. “You’d be crazy not to,” she says. “You’ve just got to use that as a learning experience, at the end of the day.” Adelaide star Ebony Marinoff, another competition stalwart, says taming the rampant Roos is the priority. “You’ve just got to keep striving,” the 28-year-old says.



“At the end of the day you have to be able to respect and honour what North Melbourne has been able to do. “I’m a competitor but at the end of the day when someone is successful … there’s so much respect there for what you’ve been able to do. “And having been coached under Crocs [North Melbourne coach Darren Crocker, who also led the Australian coaching contingent against Ireland] for the last few days, you can understand why he’s so successful. His story-telling was incredible, just the way that he expressed himself and got around …. the whole of the group,” she said. “They’re very lucky to have him at the helm. “[While] I think anyone can be beaten, it’s going to be hard to stop them.



“They have so much depth amongst their list, but I think for all of us you’ve just got to keep striving.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Misdirected or misleading? Health boss in hot water over estimates show
World.content:
Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: the estimates comments which struck a nerve (or got a laugh), police union spills tea on government talks, and a brewing mystery in the Tower of Power. The joy that is budget estimates delivered no shortage of the usual for senior unelected officials: government protection, bizarre opposition gotcha efforts, and the occasional eye-opening answer. But one director-general’s doozy seems to have struck a nerve – and frustrated someone in their orbit enough to pick up the phone to pose the question: did David Rosengren mislead his hearing? Queensland Health director-general David Rosengren at Tuesday’s estimates hearing. Queensland parliament We ran the ruler last week over the Queensland Health chief’s explanation for having three hospital and health service boards without a legally required First Nations director.



In case you missed that, Rosengren said the vacancies were the “unscheduled” result of resignations “subsequent to” the process of the March HHS board overhaul. The facts suggest otherwise. At Metro North (the state’s largest HHS) and Metro South (no.2, with the largest Indigenous population), three directors were either handed midterm marching orders or gave earlier notice. Up on the Sunshine Coast, Circus has learned that not only did Bundjalung man Terry Bell not resign after the recent recruitment round, but that he had reapplied for the board. Twice! It’s all been enough to drive one board insider, who we’ve granted anonymity to get around the fact they’re unauthorised to speak publicly, to get us on the blower and call the situation out.



They confirmed the detail about Bell’s efforts to remain on the board, and said it appeared Rosengren had “misled the estimates committee”, suggesting he should explain or apologise. Related Article Public service LNP-sponsor data centre firm taps ex-premier to join major meetings Not a minor thing, given parliamentary rules leave any deliberate misleading of proceedings by MPs open to a contempt finding. Let alone the maximum seven-year penalty for anyone else giving false evidence to parliament under the Criminal Code. Circus is, of course, not suggesting Rosengren is guilty of any such thing. Only that his evidence did not align with the facts as we understand them, and he has to date given no explanation as to why. In our generosity, we’d also posit that he was perhaps misinformed by three separate HHS boards.



For their part, we’ve sung out to the four former directors and have either been unable to reach them or found them politely declining to speak about both their departures or Rosengren’s remarks. We also put the insider’s assessment to Rosengren via the Queensland Health media team on Monday, along with a nudge for the still unanswered questions from last week. “To protect the privacy of individual applicants and comply with confidentiality obligations, Queensland Health is not able to provide specific details regarding the board recruitment process,” came the week-in-the-making response from a department spokesperson. For what it’s worth, Health Minister Tim Nicholls’ office reckons it’s all a matter for the bureaucrats – a bit rich given the ultimate appointment decisions are ones for him. While Circus is loath to share official backgrounding, such spin work in this case has sought to explain the “unscheduled” labelling of the gaps, but not the resignation element. Read into that what you will.



And the estimates comedy award goes too... Elsewhere across the 70 hours and 15 minutes of hearings over nine days, there were at last a few successful efforts to break the stuffy (or petty) nature of proceedings with some humour. But it was hard to look past the deadpanned delivery of Department of Sport, Racing and Olympic and Paralympic Games director-general Andrew Hopper as the gold standard. Department of Sport, Racing and Olympic and Paralympic Games director-general (and funny guy) Andrew Hopper. Queensland Parliament One pressure-release came after two minutes of bickering sparked by a question from Kurwongbah Labor MP Shane King about 2025-26 advertising campaigns.



This topic was the trigger for countless points of order by government MPs across the fortnight, a campaign led by Leader of the House Dr Christian Rowan. Related Article Perspective

Queensland government Five key questions that went unanswered in the first week of Qld’s scrutiny show King ultimately labelled Rowan’s efforts in this circumstance “frivolous”, which the member for Moggill took as personally offensive and had withdrawn. Speaker Pat Weir managed to dam the duelling interruptions long enough to give the call to Hopper. “My apologies, member, there was a bit going on there. Could you please repeat the question,” the department head quipped with the slightest hint of a smirk. Cue bipartisan laughter.



For contrast, Hopper’s earlier request for clarification from Labor’s opposition sports spokesperson Glenn Butcher during a line of questioning about the delayed government sport strategy was among the most cutting. Hopper: “Just to clarify, you are asking if there was money allocated in 2025-26 for a strategy that has been released today. I will take a moment for that.” After turning to speak to a colleague for all of 10 seconds, he continued: “Member, obviously with the release of the strategy in the financial year 2026-27, that is where the money is allocated.” No laughter from the chamber at that zinger. What government and police chief told union crowd



Among all the estimates fun, it would be excusable if we missed the release of the Winter 2026 edition of the Queensland Police Union Journal. But thanks to a reminder from some eagle-eyed members of the tent, we were able to catch up on all the juicy goss from the annual coppers’ collective council meeting back in May. Inside were speeches (and Q&A sessions) from acting Commissioner Brett Pointing, Premier David Crisafulli and Police Minister Dan Purdie, dutifully transcribed and published in full. And what did the political leaders and top brass have to tell union president Shane Prior’s troops? A bit of that has already been aired by our Campbell Street comrades, including approval from Crisafulli to collecting more DNA from youth offenders and supporting changes to pursuit laws.



Beyond that, Pointing also said cabinet had asked him to “come back with a model that would work better with the troops” on controversial instant domestic violence orders. Dubbed police protection directions, and earlier decried by Prior as too onerous for use in most cases, Pointing conceded the powers had not “been as effective as we had all hoped it would be”. Then police minister Bill Byrne and Deputy Commissioner Brett Pointing in 2017. Amy Mitchell-Whittington “Whilst that is still cabinet in confidence, the model that we put up, if we get it through, I think will make a huge difference,” Pointing said. Another comment from the top brass that caught Circus’ eye was the fact, in his words, that “hardly a day goes by that Shane doesn’t ring”, particularly with about watchhouse and fleet concerns.



Despite all the backslapping, some more pointed elements of the gathering were captured in the questions from delegates and elsewhere in the journal. With the government spruiking of record spending in key frontline workforces, Prior’s opening comments describe the Crisafulli LNP’s 2026-27 budget as a “pretty bland affair … a bit like reheating Monday night’s dinner on Wednesday”. Regardless, Circus imagines Crisafulli and Co will be invited back – and show up – next year. Cold water poured on brewing mystery at 1WS With all the talk of stationery supplies being slashed as part of the Crisafulli government’s bid to find $500 million in public service savings, the case of the diminishing tea bag stock in One William Street has invoked fears for many.



Circus spies were quick to raise the alarm after tea bags, milk and sugar satchels ran dry in recent weeks, with staff fearing the austerity measures had come for the much-loved cuppa. The government insists the future of the smoko brew is safe, but how do they explain the missing bags and single-serve sweeteners? Public servants get access to automatic coffee machines for a small fee inside the Tower of Power, with the coins amassed through the machines used to stock tea stations. iStock The empty kitchens were caused by end-of-life coffee machines being replaced, Circus was told. You see, public servants get access to automatic coffee machines for a small fee inside the Tower of Power, with the coins amassed through the machines used to stock tea stations. But the older machines, which only accept coins, have been pulled from the building to make way for newer models which allow electronic payments.



Meanwhile, there’s no change floating around to pay for the depleted stock of tea, milk and sugar. As a tea-and-coffee-loving column on the side of our hard-working public servants, Circus pressed the relevant minister on the issue, Public Works Minister Sam O’Connor, whose spokeswoman sought to ease concerns. “Despite the brewing speculation, there is no change to the tea and coffee arrangements for staff at 1 William Street,” she said in response to questions. Thank goodness. Now, time to put the kettle on. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email us on m.dennien@nine.com.au or james.hall@nine.com.au. World.title: We went to Panda Mart’s first Queensland store so you don’t have to
World.content:
The Queensland launch of discounted retail chain Panda Mart sparked a frenzy of shoppers, with thousands descending on the store in Brisbane’s south. The chain, described as “Temu in real life”, stocks everything from cosmetics and toys to homewares, furniture, sporting goods, outdoor gear and more. Panda Mart in Rocklea has 18 checkout counters, all of which had a line on Monday afternoon. A staff member, not authorised to speak publicly and who asked not to be named, said he served at least 1000 customers at his counter alone over the weekend.



“18 counters and 1000 people through each,” he said. “More than 1000 I reckon, I’m not sure though. It’s just a lot of people. On Saturday, Sunday it’s more. People coming in every two minutes. Panda Mart has officially opened at Rocklea in Brisbane’s south. Dominique Tassell “Every time you look over there, it’s just people, it never settles down.” The worker estimated there were 60 to 70 per cent more people on Saturday and Sunday than on Monday.



Just after midday on Monday, limited parking had forced customers to drive off-road and on the sidewalk before piling into the store located at the old Bunnings site. Cars were parked in every available space on the lawns – up on the curbs, and on every side street for at least three blocks. By 2pm, a line had formed at the door with entry staggered by staff to a few at a time. Shelves were bare for some items, with the most popular products being snacks, makeup, and furniture. Shoppers who visited the store over the weekend shared footage online of messy aisles, particularly in the rug section of the store.



Rugs were strewn across the floor in piles, blocking the aisles so no one could walk through. Related Article Retail We shop at ‘Temu in real life’. Are the products safe? Panda Mart first launched in South Africa in 2010, and launched in Victoria last year. Crowds were so large at the Cranbourne store opening in Melbourne’s outskirts that police had to be called. Police were not required at the Rocklea store during its soft opening weekend. The chain’s Victorian stores were ordered to stop trading for 72 hours by Consumer Affairs Victoria last December, while allegedly unsafe goods were seized.



In January, 147 criminal charges were laid by the consumer watchdog against Panda Mart Cranbourne for selling unsafe products. Panda Mart Cranbourne also faces 130 charges over allegedly unsafe lamps and other electrical products after scrutiny from Energy Safe Victoria. Items seized from the Victorian stores include toys and baby rattles with button batteries, which can kill or seriously injure a child if swallowed. In March, further items were seized including flammable candleholders banned in Australia due to burns and fire risks.
