World.title: Here is your mission Ben Carroll. Your time starts now.
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Here is your mission Ben Carroll. Your time starts now. August 3, 2026 — 7:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cathy Wilcox To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. VICTORIAN GOVERNMENT The main issue that Premier Ben Carroll has to deal with is not the legacy of alleged corruption of ‘the Big Build’, nor the spectre of One Nation and a weakened Liberal party coalition. It is not even the unions such as the teachers and CFMEU, nor is it the budget blowout.

It is time. That is his enemy. An election is just months away, and he has to convince Victorians that the ship can be righted and that it can head in a different direction.

Imagine if the SRL had a different push. Imagine the priority became the western end and the airport rail. Imagine if money was actually spent on infrastructure in the western suburbs where it was desperately needed. Imagine if Warragul got the hospital it was promised over 30 years ago. Imagine if public housing and school upgrades were deemed essential and were funded.

Let’s hope Ben Carroll has some imagination and will deliver on any promises he makes, unlike previous premiers.

Labor deserves a kick in the pants. Does Victoria deserve a bickering Liberal party and a right wing One Nation coalition instead? That is the choice at the moment. Only time, Carroll’s enemy, will tell.

Greg Tuck, Warragul The airport rail that got away

Victorians recall with regret the Allan government’s announcement postponing the Airport Rail project. It was in the same 2024 budget that affirmed a $26 billion price tag for the North East Link, after its $10 billion blowout was revealed in December 2023. It doesn’t take much imagination to conclude the one followed directly from the other.

Had someone asked the Parliamentary Budget Office how much could be saved by cancelling the North East Link and downing tools right then, I’m sure they’d have dutifully tallied the billions in hypothetical, avoided construction and operating costs over subsequent decades.

It would not have un-bulldozed 20,000 trees or restored the open wounds sliced through the Yarra and Koonung valleys - but maybe we’d have got airport rail on its original timetable.

When it comes to stopping fiscal and environmental loss from big projects, there really only is one right time, and that’s at the original decision to proceed or not. For these decisions to serve the public interest it’s necessary that they tick all the ‘process’ boxes but as we’ve seen, not sufficiently enough.

There must be a transparent assessment of their merits, including in comparison to good-faith alternatives.

Tony Morton, president, Public Transport Users Association



Not too late to provide statewide tree measures

I read with interest the article ″⁣I cried when the council cut down the tree by my house″⁣, 30/7. Trees, whether they are located on public or private land are valuable assets and play a vital role in cooling our cities in a warming climate.

In ‘Plan for Victoria’, the state’s blueprint on how Victoria will grow over time, the state government has set a target of 30 per cent tree canopy cover in urban areas.

That isn’t an arbitrary number; it’s widely accepted nationally and internationally as the minimum amount of cover necessary for human health and wellbeing.

In September 2025, the state government introduced statewide provisions over the protection of trees. Whilst welcome, it was disappointing that in July this year the state government removed a long-standing Significant Landscape Overlay - Schedule 9 (SLO9) in the City of Whitehorse which was a proven, readily enforceable local protection of trees on private land.

From a legal perspective there is no reason why both statewide and local provisions cannot co-exist and complement one another. Whitehorse Council is confident that SLO9 will not undermine housing supply targets. I urge the state government to reintroduce SLO9 in the Whitehorse Planning Scheme.

Yvonne Bowyer, Surrey Hills THE FORUM Carroll’s conversion

As our new premier moves with lightning speed to disassociate himself from his two predecessors by promising a government of integrity, fiscal prudence and a constructive relationship with business, some of us remain to be convinced,

If he had such strong beliefs and convictions, one could ask why did he continue to serve as both a senior minister and deputy premier committed to advocating the policies implemented by those from whom he now distances himself.

A politician of true conviction would have resigned from cabinet and retreated to the backbench. The cynic would suggest the imminent election, with the prospect of being consigned to opposition irrelevance without the rewards of office, are responsible for Carroll’s “road to Damascus” conversion.

Bob Hawke said any politician who underestimates the intelligence and common sense of Australian voters is a fool: we await November for confirmation or contradiction of that statement.

William Vickers, Melbourne Tim Wilson’s past

I was interested to read Deborah Snow’s profile of my local member, Tim Wilson “Second Coming”, Good Weekend, 1/8. I was unsurprised to read that “his superpower is shamelessness”; though the most shameless episode in our member’s life went unreported.

During his years at the Institute of Public Affairs, Wilson several times in writing criticised and ridiculed the Human Rights Commission and the then Human Rights Commissioner.

However, when the Abbott government came to power and George Brandis offered him the position of Human Rights Commissioner, he took it straightaway.

Not just that, but he spent a couple of years gallivanting around Australia and elsewhere at enormous cost.

At the time, many people simply couldn’t believe he had taken the HRC job and thought it was a joke. Unfortunately, it wasn’t.

Tony Adami, Caulfield South White Australia’s end

Apropos George Brandis’ column ″⁣Tony Abbott recalls a whiter Australia than I do, Menzies rejected his version, as do many Liberals″⁣ (3/8), I recall at the start of the 1961 election, Melbourne University students decided to put repeal of the White Australia policy on the agenda.

As usual, prime minister Bob Menzies was to give his policy speech at Kew Town Hall. The students decided to attend the meeting to raise the issue. Some of us in the Eureka Youth League, heard about this so we joined in, and dressed well as Young Liberals, to not arouse suspicion, and many of us occupied the back of the hall. When Menzies started we all began chanting about repeal of the White Australia Policy and Menzies was drowned out.

After that, he said he would never again give his policy speech in a public hall.

I acknowledge the part played by Menzies, Holt, followed by Malcolm Fraser, as important, but those students finally got the disgraceful policy onto the agenda in a big way, with wide media coverage, as this was the beginning of the end.

Max Ogden, Fitzroy North



Albanese’s timidity

Anthony Albanese’s gambling reforms demonstrate a timidity in leadership. While arguing that Labor’s proposed reforms balance the need to protect children from gambling ads while preserving adults’ freedom to bet, it actually smacks of dancing to the tune of vested interests.

Australia is caught up in a pernicious web of gambling, and governments of all persuasions have become partners in the social harm gambling causes by its reliance on gambling tax revenues. Gambling is a regressive form of taxation. The current level of gambling undermines the country’s social fabric. It redirects “wealth” from broad-based society into the hands of a few who continue to manipulate all levels of society and government.

It’s not about preserving an adults’ freedom to bet. You do not need advertising to be able to bet, and you certainly don’t need gambling advertising blatantly recruiting children for its future market. All 31 recommendations of the Murphy inquiry should be accepted.

David Conolly, Brighton Two state impasse

Your correspondent (Letters, 3/8) is right, Netanyahu doesn’t want a two-state solution, but not for the reasons your correspondent thinks. On multiple occasions, Israel has offered the Palestinians generous offers of statehood – and every time this was rejected for one simple reason.

Hamas, indeed many Palestinians, do not recognise Israel’s right to exist, in fact, the terrorist group’s constitution stipulates this.

Even the more moderate Palestinian Authority rewards terrorism via their Martyrs Fund.

Israel is fighting an existential threat from Hamas, Iran and Hezbollah, while Egypt and Jordan decided long ago they preferred peace rather than war.

Julie Krousoratis, Bulleen Pump price ride

With the fuel excise now fully restored, the fuel stations have been warned by the treasurer (3/8) that the ACCC will monitor pump prices for any unwarranted increases.

What has the ACCC actually done to ensure “fair” fuel prices over the years? I would suggest very little because over the past 30 years, I can recall prices increasing astronomically just before every school holiday, every long weekend, each Easter and Christmas and, way back in 2000, rising steeply just before the Sydney Olympics.

So what has changed, that will now see the ACCC bring the fuel industry to account?

Phil Mackenzie, Eaglemont Expert urgent care

The front page headline in the Sunday Age (″⁣Doctors pan urgent care clinics″⁣, 2/8) almost had me choking on my cornflakes. I had been bitten by a dog the night before and had been persuaded by my family to get some antibiotic cover. As it was Saturday night, and my wounds weren’t severe, a first-time visit to a nearby urgent care clinic seemed a sensible idea.

There, after having my medical history recorded and checked against the government record, I was triaged by a nurse, then seen by the doctor, given a tetanus injection, the script for an antibiotic and even the address of the nearest late-night pharmacy. So that they didn’t miss out on anything, I was also advised to see my GP for a check-up in a few days. I was out the door in 95 minutes.

When I had arrived, there had been nine people in the waiting area. When I left, there was a new group. For the GPs’ organisation to say that urgent care clinics are ″⁣doing absolutely nothing″⁣ to ease the pressure on hospital emergency departments, can only be described as ridiculous, or in self-interest.

Jeffrey Newman, Ivanhoe In your dreams

Two letters (3/8) from dreamers for flying cars. Perhaps they should do a small course in energy used to get from A to B compared with a mass transit system.

And, while modern cars are quite efficient at reducing passenger trauma in a collision, it’s hard to imagine a system that protects the flyers from a fall from the heights needed to get the necessary travel corridor flow.

Laurie Comerford, Chelsea



Fires made worse

I’m tired of people blaming arson, lack of back burning and other marginal factors for bushfires clearly driven by an escalating climate crisis (Letters, “Europe on fire”, 3/8). These arguments come straight from the fossil fuel company playbook to delay action. Researchers at World Weather Attribution found that climate change made the recent hot, dry, windy conditions in Spain around 20 times more likely. They also concluded that the recent extreme European heatwave simply would not have occurred without human-driven warming. That heatwave killed 20,000 people.

The blame sits squarely with the coal, oil and gas companies and the governments who enable the continuation of the damaging pollution they cause. Shame on them.

Amy Hiller, Kew Fires harder to stop

Whilst your correspondent is correct that human activity started most of Europe’s recent wildfires, it should be noted that Australia’s 2019-2020 Black Summer forest fires, whose scale was unprecedented both in an Australian and global context, were primarily caused by dry lightning.

The reality is that regardless of their cause, once started wildfires are now likely to be harder to extinguish due to ongoing climate change. Thus, particularly in the extratropics, there have been dramatic increases over recent decades in the area burned by wildfires, in their intensity, and in the length of the fire season.

Geoff Feren, St Kilda East Abbott’s exclamation

When will Tony Abbott do the right thing and publicly admit that he was wrong to denounce climate change as ″⁣absolute crap″⁣ in 2009? Shame on him and the party that appointed him its chairman.

Juliet Flesch, Kew Keep it beautiful

Living in rural Victoria, I watch in horror as the litter piles up along roadsides.

Having grown up in the 1970s I recall the Keep Australia Beautiful campaign, which made me believe that change is possible.

I wonder why there appears to be no effort towards managing this current, calamitous situation that I realise is complex, but history has proven can be rectified. Please can we have immediate action?

Sharyn Cook, Wimmera AND ANOTHER THING



Real estate

″⁣Property price slump deepens: Melbourne remains the weakest market in the nation″⁣ (3/8). Well, I’m no economist, but surely that can be rephrased as: ″⁣Housing becomes more affordable in Victoria″⁣? Caroline Williamson, Brunswick Am I the only reader sick of seeing articles about the lives of Antony Catalano and Luke Sayers?

Ann Maginness, Beaumaris Furthermore

I don’t trust any Trump-declared Gaza deal. I don’t trust Hamas’ promise to completely disarm. I do trust the likelihood of Israeli PM Netanyahu breaking the deal on some imagined or concocted provocation, however flimsy.

Kevin Burke, Sandringham Using AI and a bit of luck, the SRL could do a left turn out to Tullamarine airport – a loop so near and surely it’s not too late ?

Margaret Skeen, Ocean Grove



If poorer families can’t allow members to go to uni, perhaps those with excess money made from property could help out?

Bruce Dudon, Woodend I’ve just seen Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey. Still a bit unsure. Were they from Los Angeles or New York?

Philip Henseleit, Glenlee The best consequence of an Australian republic? No more shrill demands for ″⁣royal” commissions!

Peter Bennett, Clifton Hill Gina Rinehart is a flesh and blood person, not a punching bag. Shame on the ABC TV for the comments aired on Race Around The World, which were outrageous, hurtful, demeaning and frankly, disgusting.

Sally Dobson, South Melbourne Re youth crime: perhaps it’s time to take a leaf out of the US justice book and lock up irresponsible parents.

George Stockman, Bendigo



Finally

Growing up in Ashburton in the 70s, my family was fortunate enough to be under the care of a new, young dentist, Lesley Aisen. And today (Letters, 3/8) my suspicions were confirmed – he is the regular contributor to The Age. I am now basking in some reflected glory!

Julie Blackwood, Chelsea The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ‘Forgotten victim’ in Keli Lane saga speaks out
World.content:
The adult daughter of convicted killer Keli Lane says she is a forgotten victim of her mother’s ongoing detention and has urged her release on parole with more than two years remaining on her sentence.

“I am a forgotten victim in this situation,” the now 25-year-old daughter wrote in a letter to authorities, provided to Nine’s A Current Affair program.

Convicted killer Keli Lane pictured with her daughter, who now aged 25, is urging for her mother’s release on parole. A Current Affair

“My hope is simple: that my mum can come home and that I can spend meaningful time with her, that is all I wish for.”

She recalled being dropped at school by her mother when she was nine years old, the last time she saw her before Lane was taken into custody after being convicted of the 1996 murder of her baby daughter Tegan.

World.title: The ugly family feud that threatens to upend this US election race
World.content:
Graphic content WorldNorth AmericaUS midterm elections The ugly family feud that threatens to upend this US election race Annie Karni August 3, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content Washington: US Republican senator Bernie Moreno broke his silence on Sunday (Washington time) about a years-long family drama involving domestic abuse allegations against his former son-in-law, Republican congressman Max Miller, saying in an emotional statement that Miller was not fit to hold public office. Moreno, saying the dispute had put his family through “pure hell”, scathingly denounced Miller, whose ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused him of abusing her and their two-year-old daughter. Congressman Max Miller of Ohio has denied the accusations and vowed that he is “not getting out of this race”. Bloomberg “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” Bernie Moreno wrote in a post on the social platform X. He added: “I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter.”



He continued: “He should not serve in the House of Representatives. I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake. I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does.” Related Article Analysis

US election Trump lays the groundwork for emergency declaration ahead of midterms The Ohio senator issued his statement in reaction to an earlier, defiant livestream on Sunday by Miller, who is seeking re-election in Ohio’s 7th Congressional District. Miller denied the accusations and vowed that he was “not getting out of this race”. Miller is running in a tight race in what had been a safe seat for Republicans before the allegations became public. Moreno’s statement, his first on the issue, seems likely to further damage Miller’s campaign, a source of concern for Republicans nationally even as they have largely maintained public silence. The wrenching public back-and-forth came just three days before the deadline for Republicans to replace Miller on the ballot – or risk locking him in as the GOP nominee for a seat that has become competitive in large part because of the allegations against him. Miller appears to be just 1 percentage point ahead of his Democratic challenger, according to internal polling research by Democrats, in a district that US President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024.



Until now, Republicans across the board have chosen not to denounce Miller or call for his resignation, dismissing the charges against him as mere “allegations”. It was not clear on Sunday how Moreno’s weighing in would shift the response from other Republicans. In a roughly 20-minute livestream, Miller categorically denied all the accusations that Emily Moreno has levelled at him in court. He also claimed that she had “significant mental health challenges”, without offering any evidence. Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio says the dispute has put his family through “pure hell”. AP Photo/Allison Robbert Miller said he had never scalded Moreno’s chest and stomach by throwing hot water from a skillet at her body, as she has accused him, dismissing the incident as “horseplay in our kitchen” with water that was not boiling. He also denied her accusation that he held a gun to her head, and he vehemently rejected her charge that he had fractured their daughter’s collarbone and bruised her shoulder.



Miller, a former staff member for Trump, blamed his daughter’s injuries on two daycare workers. Related Article US election Can a left-wing Muslim win the Midwest? Or are Democrats about to make a big mistake “If these accusations were true, I would be in jail,” Miller said, seated in his kitchen and reading haltingly from a script. He contended that the credibility of her assertions was undermined by the fact that he still retains joint custody after years of court battles. In his livestream, Miller repeatedly pointed to examples of what he claimed were friendly overtures from Moreno as proof that she was fabricating the claims of abuse. “If I had assaulted her, would she have offered to cook me dinner six days later?” he asked. Moreno is seeking to end their shared parenting agreement. The issue is expected to go to court on November 5. Last week, Moreno filed a restraining order against Miller, claiming he had harassed and threatened her lawyers.



Immediately after his livestream, Miller made public a trove of recordings, text message exchanges and court documents that he said would prove his innocence. A lawyer for Moreno did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump’s entered a new phase: the unmaking of his presidency Bruce Wolpe Senior fellow at the US Studies Centre and former political staffer Amid broad silence from Republicans, Democrats have called for a House ethics committee investigation into the allegations against Miller. Speaker Mike Johnson has said only that there is an ethics process for handling such accusations. He did not respond to a request for comment on Sunday. Republican congressman Jim Jordan, also from Ohio, defended Miller in a recent interview. “This is a family matter. I know Max is a good man,” he told CNN. “I hope he wins re-election.” Behind the scenes, however, Republicans in Trump’s orbit have said they are alarmed by Miller’s decision to go on the offensive against Moreno and are concerned about his re-election campaign.



Miller, however, expressed deep confidence on Sunday that he would be back in Congress next year. “This election to me is about my family and about our daughter and keeping our values here and holding the media and other individuals accountable,” he said. Emily Moreno is not the first woman to level domestic abuse allegations against Miller. In her memoir, Stephanie Grisham, a former White House press secretary, wrote that she dated someone in the administration who was physically abusive. She later acknowledged that she had been referring to Miller. If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: ‘Can’t keep kids safe’: Inherent risks in market-driven childcare
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaEducation ‘Can’t keep kids safe’: Inherent risks in market-driven childcare Nicole Precel August 3, 2026 — 7:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Childcare worker Sherry used to wake up every morning unsure of how to keep the 11 children in her care safe. “It hurts me as a teacher that you can’t keep the children in your care safe,” she said. “It’s stressful and overwhelming.” Lauren Treweek with sons Gus, 1, who goes to daycare, and Xavier, 3, who goes to kinder. Joe Armao The 30-year-old, who asked not to use her surname to speak openly, said challenging behaviours, a one-to-11 ratio and little support from management made it an impossible job and inherently risky. A report from Victoria University’s Mitchell Institute found the push to expand childcare had created workforce churn, provider turnover and growing risk.



Since 2013, 40.7 per cent of for-profit centres have changed operators, some as many as five times, the report shows. Analysis of the workforce found the median hourly wage for educators is akin to cleaners – $34.30, compared with $62 for schoolteachers. It is below the median hourly wage of $42.40. The most recent data from the Australian Taxation Office (2022/2023) shows 52 per cent of jobs in the childcare sector were held for less than a year. To compound the lack of continuity, large for-profit private providers (with more than 25 centres) were more than three times as likely to have an enforcement action recorded than centres run by not-for-profit or community providers.



Mitchell Institute director Professor Peter Hurley said using markets to boost childcare places while keeping prices down had come at a cost. “These approaches bake-in the deficiencies of low pay and high turnover and put enormous strain on the sector. They end up rewarding those providers who can produce an hour of care in the cheapest way possible while meeting the minimum standards,” he said. Lauren Treweek with her sons, Xavier, 3, and Gus, 1. Joe Armao Childcare centres receive childcare subsidy payments from the federal government ($16.9 billion in 2025-26) on behalf of families to deliver reduced-cost services. Closures and new centres are driven by the market. Hurley said the report, The price of a place: Instability, risk and the hidden cost of Australia’s early childhood education and care system, showed that the market had reduced barriers for operators to easily open or close centres.



“[Providers] can trial the market, and if it doesn’t work, they can leave,” he said. Mitchell Institute director Peter Hurley. Ruby Alexander. “That can work with something like an airline industry. When it comes to children, they’re extremely vulnerable. One of the things that really struck me with these horrible cases that’s been going on is just how many places they’ve worked,” he said. “That’s prompted us to look at this. The shorter nature of the employment and educators.” Major changes have been introduced since the childcare sector was plunged into crisis in July last year when horrific allegations of child sex abuse surfaced across Australia.



In Melbourne, accused childcare rapist Joshua Dale Brown is facing more than 100 charges, including sexually penetrating multiple children he was employed to care for. In Sydney, daycare worker Hamish Tait, 35, is facing more than 320 charges over his alleged abuse of more than 150 children. There’s since been a Victorian parliamentary inquiry, a shift in the Working With Children Check, tightening of market entry requirements, and the ability to suspend or cancel subsidy payments for serious breaches. The Front Project chief executive officer, Caroline Croser-Barlow, said recent measures to improve quality, such as stripping centres of the childcare subsidy for ongoing breaches, and worker-retention payments, had produced improvements. “Do I think we’ve done enough? Absolutely not.” The worst operators were those seeking to flip centres and profit, she said.



The amount of childcare places has almost doubled since 2013, from about 400,000 to about 730,000 - almost entirely by private for-profit providers who account for 74 per cent of long daycare places, the research shows. The Parenthood’s Georgie Dent said early education should be funded more like schools, as core public infrastructure, not a market to be left to its own devices. “That means funding that reflects the actual cost of delivering high-quality education and care: fair wages, stable staffing, professional development and safe facilities,” she said.



Mother-of-three Lauren Treweek said for parents, long daycare continued to be “unbelievably and astronomically expensive” amid “quite honestly terrifying stories”. “It seems like every time you get a break, in terms of the rebate being changed, the private centres just end up putting their fees up, or to be honest, centres in general,” she said. Treweek tried to get two of her children into the same childcare centre but couldn’t, so now has to do three separate drop-offs: one-year-old Gus at long daycare, Xavier, 3, to kindergarten, and Sienna, 5, to school. She said the short tenure of educators was concerning, as was a lack of transparency from operators. “How can you build trust in educators when they’re not even at the centre for a year, or the minute you drop your child off, you’re hoping for this great relationship, as they have with your family, and then, you know, six to 12 months later, they’re not there?” she said.



“I think the visibility that parents are being provided with is terrible. It’s shocking,” she said. Minister for Early Childhood Education Jess Walsh said the government was consulting on a national early education and care commission, which could help guide a path towards universal early childhood education and care, address undersupply and oversupply, and build a stronger system. Education ministers are due to meet to discuss its development in October. She said a 15 per cent pay rise for educators was stabilising the workforce, and states and territories were investing about half-a-billion dollars to support a package of reforms to lift safety and standards across the sector.



Hurley said it wasn’t for-profit centres that were the issue, but the childcare model itself, which required more research into alternatives. Childcare worker Sherry has moved to a sessional kindergarten. “It’s different. It’s not-for-profit, so I feel like the service is actually putting effort into supporting children,” she said. “Every service will say it’s children-centred, but in practice, it’s not. It’s profit-centred. Editor's pick Exclusive

Domestic violence WA watchdog probes police interactions with Virginia Giuffre



“We put children at risk. We put educators at risk as well.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Wellington residents shocked by 'ridiculous' water bills for car parks, granny flats
World.content:
Wellington residents have questions over new water costs Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Wellington region residents say they've been handed "ridiculous" and "unreasonable" water bills for basement car parks and granny flats.

There's been shock and confusion for some Wellington residents, as households started receiving the separate bills last week.

Water bills are set to increase on average by 13.3 percent this year for residents. Previously incorporated into council rates, Wellington's mayor said people will see that component removed from their next council rates' bill.

Wellington City resident Ceridwyn Roberts said she received two water bills last week - one for her apartment, and one for her basement car park.

Her apartment bill was about $380 for the quarter, she said, while her car park bill was $89.

"I don't mind paying for water, but this seems ridiculous.

"This seems completely antithetical to what they're trying to do, surely, because surely what's happening is a. we need to pay for the water pipes and b) we need to decrease the use of water."

Roberts said while there's a small tap in the room, she personally doesn't use water from it - though it might get used to fill up something occasionally.

She said there wasn't any stormwater run-off from the car park, and no sewage coming from it.

A Lower Hutt resident, who RNZ agreed not to name, said she was shocked to see her water bill was $1079.07 for the quarter.

She said after looking into her bill and Tiaki Wai's website, she's seeing a double set of charges, due to a granny flat on her property where her mother-in-law lives.

The resident said the granny flat shares the plumbing connection for the toilet, shower and sink, with the main house.

"I view it as really unreasonable ... there's only one connection that everything goes through. So it seems like we're being double charged for that connection. You know, anything that happens to the water beyond the toby is our thing to deal with."

A quarterly bill of over $1000 was too much, she said.

"It's wrong .. I don't understand how something can cost that much for, you know, having three people in one household to use that much water usage."

Error in Lower Hutt residents' payment system

Lower Hutt resident Dani Garvey said she wanted to pay her water bill in weekly payments throughout the year.

Last week, Tiaki Wai's chief customer officer Liza Gunn said residents would not have to pay full amounts of quarterly payments by 1 September if they set up a direct debit with Tiaki Wai.

But Garvey tried to do this, and was told she couldn't, she said.

She had first gone to Tiaki Wai's website and been directed to the Payble app - but was unable to set up weekly payments across the year.

"I called Tiaki Wai, and followed their prompts and got put through the rates team at Hutt City Council, who's apparently the payments team, they tried to do a regular weekly payment, based on the annual amount, in many different ways - their system would not allow it."

Her first quarter bill was about $562 - she said - and if she could pay weekly that would work out to between $42 and $46 per week, rather than $140 per week.

She said $140 is "huge" in a cost of living crisis.

"It has been stressful.

"The fact that they haven't given the full, annual amount in my initial invoice, and they're effectively trying to force me to pay $140 a week - it seems like it's extortion."

In a statement, Gunn said Hutt City Council was aware of an issue on the Payble App - and staff were trying to fix it.

"It's a configuration quirk at this point that we are working quickly to resolve.

"We also have a message up on our HCC Payble page to this effect, and we will have a resolution as soon as possible."

She said she didn't recommend people sign up to regular payments until it was sorted, and updates would be made on the website.

Gunn said Roberts' water bill for the car park was likely due to stormwater infrastructure charging - though there may be a drinking water charge too, if there's a tap in the car park.

Tiaki Wai board chair Will Peet. Supplied / Tiaki Wai

"Stormwater charges help fund the whole network that manages rainwater across the customer's area; not just pipes.

"This includes maintaining, repairing and upgrading all types of stormwater infrastructure that collects and carries runoff and helps reduce flood risk across the area."

Tiaki Wai board chair Will Peet said water charges are increasing on average, by about 13 percent for the region's residents this year.

He said the new entity has inherited the four Wellington councils' water charging systems.

Porirua, Upper and Lower Hutt have a fixed water charge, with a small amount based on property value. Wellington city council has been basing water charges on property value, not usage, he said.

World.title: Dunedin city councillor asked to leave two public events in a week
World.content:
Controversial Dunedin city councillor Benedict Ong has been kicked out of a council meeting to discuss amalgamation plans and has been asked to leave two public events in the past week.

Ong has faced several code of conduct complaints and has been suspended from some council duties because of his behaviour.

He was asked to leave a student protest on 29 July and a health debate in Dunedin on 1 August.

At the start of Monday's council meeting, Ong placed a copy of William Golding's Lord of the Flies in front of him on the table in the council chambers.

He later questioned the value of council assets before a point of order was called by councillor Steve Walker who said he was being disrespectful to staff.

Ong said the council's commercial assets were "tremendously undervalued" and "not performing financially" and asked staff for an indication of the "valuation of our dowry" ahead of a "potential marriage" with another council.

General manager of city services Scott MacLean said the council was not at the point where it was starting to divvy up or value assets and it was far too early to say how they would be managed.

Ong then asked staff if it was clear that the Otago Regional Council would be dissolved through the government's "backstop" process if the city council did not submit a voluntary amalgamation proposal.

Mayor Sophie Barker said the government had not announced what the process would look like and staff said they could not provide a professional judgement on the unknown.

Walker said the aggressive questioning of staff was "completely unacceptable", while Ong continued to talk over him.

Barker upheld the point of order and said staff had answered Ong's question and were not in a position to give an opinion, before moving on to further questions.

A short time later, Ong made a comment about the financial performance of Dunedin and Queenstown airports, before Barker asked him if he had a specific question.

"We need a valuation for this potential marriage we are being asked to agree to," Ong said.

Walker called another point of order and said Ong was "continuously bringing this meeting under disorder".

Barker told Ong he had to stop interrupting or he would have to leave. After he continued to talk over her, she told him to leave and adjourned the meeting so Ong could be removed.

"I am not leaving unless you want me to be the main topic tomorrow in the news, I don't think you want that," Ong said.

The council later voted to work with Queenstown Lakes District Council (contingent on its agreement and participation) to develop and submit a Head Start proposal in support of a two unitary model, made up of the Inland Otago Unitary Authority and a Coastal Otago Unitary Authority, with regional council functions supported through a shared services arrangement.

Speaking after the meeting, Ong said he had been "wrongfully barred, blocked and banned" from his right to vote at council meetings.

He said he was simply asking questions on behalf of ratepayers and had been prevented from doing so.

Councillor asked to leave public events

Ong was asked to leave a University of Otago student protest and a health debate hosted by the Big Hairy Network in the past week, treatment he said was politically motivated.

Education Action Group 26 organised a protest and sit-in at the university's St David's complex to protest against tertiary education cuts.

Spokesperson Annabel Hankin said it was great to see a city councillor attend the event in support of the fees-free scheme and Ong was among others who put their hands up to speak in response to a question during the sit-in.

When he was not selected, he stood up and spoke loudly, before being told to settle down and not to interrupt others.

She described his behaviour as "a little bit disorderly and distracting from what we were there for", but that it was "pretty harmless" and easily dealt with.

"This was a protest of students and university staff and community and he doesn't get any more right to speak than anyone else," she said.

Ong said he asked to speak as a council representative because Dunedin was the only council to formally oppose the government's decision to scrap the final-year fees-free tertiary policy.

He also wanted to talk about how Dunedin subsidised the university and how he did not think the institution should be building a new campus in Queenstown, but instead spending money in the city.

Ong said he was denied the chance to speak, heckled and asked to leave, but remained until he had to go to another appointment.

The Big Hairy Network held the first of several pre-election debates in Dunedin on Wednesday night, with a focus on health.

Ong said he paid $20 to attend the debate and wanted to ask questions but was denied the chance to do so because the organisers did not like him.

Debate co-organiser Mike "Chewie" Bennett said Ong was among 200 audience members who were asked to submit questions at half-time, to be presented to the the Labour, Greens, ACT and NZ First candidates during the second half of the event.

Bennett said Ong got up and asked to speak, but was told he had missed his chance because he had not put forward a question earlier as instructed and was instructed to return to his seat.

When he again asked to speak, security were called and Ong was asked to leave. Bennett said he became involved to try to de-escalate the situation.

"I said he could return to his seat as long as he was no longer disruptive to the debate," he said.

"There were lots of mentions of the fact that he's a city councillor, he represents heaps of people and I'm just like, 'no, in this forum, you're just another voter, the fact that you're a city councillor doesn't give you extra push here'."

Bennett said Ong was booed by the audience when he stood up to speak during the candidates' final statements.

World.title: Almost a million cervical cancer screening notifications not sent out, review finds
World.content:
Almost a million notifications did not get sent to people eligible for cancer screening due to flaws in the national cervical cancer screening programme, a review has found.

As a result, the system was not providing a comprehensive safety net.

A national register was launched in September 2023, along with a change to HPV primary screening instead of a smear test.

A review by a Health New Zealand expert panel, released on Monday, said the register was working satisfactorily in many ways but the clinical safety of the register could not be assured in some situations.

The register was not making contact with everyone eligible for screening due to the way it was designed, as well as unintentional flaws in the way it was built, the review said.

More than 800,000 notifications for screening were not triggered and another 160,000 notifications were triggered but not sent as of June 2025.

That included more than 600,000 notifications not sent or triggered due to people considered "inactive" because of Health NZ's "NHI active rule" that meant people who had not accessed health services for three years were not sent cervical screening eligibility information.

Others were not contacted due to postal addressees being incorrect or lacking.

A process aimed at prioritising those most in need - referred to as cohorting - also resulted in people only in the most high-priority group being contacted.

Eligibility and recall notifications were only sent to people in Cohort One - people ageing into the scheme and unscreened or underscreened Māori or Pacific people who were not enrolled in primary care.

The review made 48 recommendations, including identifying and contacting all unscreened and under-screened people as a priority.

The system needed to ensure there was appropriate follow-up when screening detected abnormalities, it said.

The register does not currently have access to complete screening histories for all participants.

This meant it might not be able to determine next steps and if additional work was required to review participants with complex histories, including previous high-grade results or other persistent HPV infections to ensure they were receiving appropriate care, the review said.

"Failure to do so poses a significant risk to affected individuals, potentially leading to delayed diagnosis or treatment and so proactive measures must be taken to safeguard patient outcomes," it said.

The review called for the National Cervical Screening Programme and Health NZ's Digital Services to develop an action plan to address the issues identified by the notification review.

National Public Health Service director prevention screening Alana Ewe-Snow said it was grateful to the work of the panel in identifying the areas for improvement.

"We acknowledge there is further work to do to improve the register. We are working hard to address the panel's recommendations. The main recommendations centred around improving clinical case review, data quality and notifications to women," Dr Ewe-Snow said.

Screening rates were higher than ever with increases across all ethnicities following the introduction of HPV primary screening with more than a million people screened since the register was introduced in September 2023, she said.

"This progress is heartening but there is much more work to do. Improvements to the register will mean we can reach even more women for screening. We'll be able to support more women to progress through the screening assessment and treatment pathway earlier."

There had been 13,000 case reviews and so far there was no indication anyone had been harmed as a result of the system's issues, Dr Ewe-Snow said.

"We are well on the way towards enacting the panel's recommendations. We've completed six already with a further 11 in progress.

"For example, we invested another $1.4 million for urgent clinical case review, clinical safety assurance and early remediation. We're committed to concluding this work within the next two years."

There were about 700 case reviews remaining, she said.

"It's mainly around managing the women with the most complex medical history and we're aiming to have those remaining 700 completed over the next couple of months."

Ewe-Snow said cervical screening was the highest it had ever been.

"Since 2023 our coverage has increased by 9.6 percent and it's now nationally at 77.3 percent. We're proud of the result that we currently have," she said.

World.title: Christchurch mum woken by stranger in child's bedroom
World.content:
Police arrested a stranger who was found inside a child's bedroom in a Christchurch house in the early hours of Sunday morning.

Officers were called to the property in Wigram after the people who lived at the house discovered the intruder.

In a post on social media, the mother said she was woken in the night by a strange man in her two-year-old's bedroom.

"Im thankful my partner dragged him out to the hallway and got him down on the ground so I could grab my son and call the police," she said.

"I never thought something like this would happen to us so it has been a very scary traumatic lesson and I am now absolutely petrified to be in my home."

The mother said she was investing in alarms and cameras as a result of the break in.

Police said the man received medical attention and no charges had been laid.

St John said a person was taken to Christchurch Hospital in a moderate condition.

World.title: Minister refuses to say if fast-track application to bulldoze golf course has been filed
World.content:
The minister and ministry overseeing fast-track projects are refusing to say if an application has been made to controversially bulldoze Canterbury's Pegasus Golf Course to make way for hundreds of homes.

Housing developer Wolfbrook bought the 18-hole, 77-hectare golf course in May and plans to redevelop the land into housing using the government's fast-track consent process.

The New Zealand Herald last week reported Wolfbrook had submitted its referral application to Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop.

But Bishop's office refused to confirm if the application had been made and referred RNZ to Wolfbrook.

Wolfbrook has ignored RNZ's repeated requests for comment on the proposal.

The Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport would also not comment about the application.

"MCERT cannot comment on whether applications have been received, are being processed or are under active consideration for referral by the Minister for Infrastructure," the ministry said in an emailed response.

"Information on referral applications is published on the fast-track website following the Minister for Infrastructure's decision to accept or decline a referral application because, before this, projects may be withdrawn or returned if found to be non-compliant, and some application details could be commercially sensitive.

"If a project is accepted for referral to the fast-track process, applicants can then lodge a substantive application for consideration by an expert panel."

More than 16,000 people signed a petition calling for the project to face the usual consenting process.

The petition was handed over to parliament in July.

That followed a public meeting in June of more than 500 people opposed to the plan for the golf course.

Wolfbrook further inflamed tensions with the community when it concreted holes at the golf course in early July.

Waimakariri MP Matt Doocey has said he opposed the project and its use of the Fast-track Approvals Act.

Waimakariri mayor Dan Gordon was also opposed and wrote a letter to Bishop urging the application be declined.

Waimakariri District Council was advised of Wolfbrook's intention to fast-track the project on 24 June.

Under the Fast-track Approvals Act the council had 20 working days to formally respond to Wolfbrook's letter.

The council told RNZ it did not formally respond but council representatives instead met with the developer to discuss the proposal.

"It's common for planning staff to meet with developers to discuss proposals, provide information about Council services (e.g. three waters) and highlight any potential issues. This meeting does not imply endorsement or otherwise of any project," the council said.

Waimakariri District Council also released to RNZ the letter notifying it of the proposal. It was sent by planning company Novo Group on behalf of Wolfbrook.

The letter said the development of the golf course would allow for up to 1000 homes and a mixed-use retail and commercial area.

"With the closure of the private golf club previously operated by Pegasus Golf Limited, Wolfbrook considers that the site presents as a logical extension of the urban area in a location that is devoid of many of the constraints that may exist in other areas of the district (e.g. development of highly productive land, development with poor access to public transport and amenities, and development within airport noise contours or high flood hazard areas)," the letter said.

"In this context, the project is proposed to deliver a master-planned extension to the Pegasus, Woodend and Ravenswood urban area, supported by integrated infrastructure, open space and supporting community and commercial services. To achieve this outcome, the project will be designed with expert input in order to leverage existing site opportunities and manage any identified adverse effects.

"Wolfbrook recognises that the site is located within a culturally significant landscape, is cognisant of the cultural overlays identified in the Waimakariri District Plan and has initiated engagement with Ngāi Tūāhuriri. Wolfbrook is committed to ongoing engagement with mana whenua in order to identify, understand and appropriately recognise and provide for cultural values and the relationship of mana whenua with the land, including wāhi tapu and other taonga.

"Overall, the project will enable and support a well-functioning urban environment by responding to strong housing demand in a strategically appropriate location whilst recognising and responding to known values and constraints."

World.title: Early childhood teacher accused of making intimate recordings faces 21 new charges
World.content:
An early childhood teacher who was arrested after a recording device was found in a staff bathroom now faces 21 more charges of making an intimate visual recording.

Police say no children have been identified in any of the recordings.

In response to earlier questions from RNZ, Detective Senior Sergeant Natalie Flowerdew-Brown confirmed police received a report that a recording device had been found in a staff bathroom at an early childcare education facility in Mount Maunganui on 30 June.

"Police conducted enquiries and a 53-year-old man was arrested in relation to the incident.

"He is due to reappear in Tauranga District Court on 3 August, charged with making an intimate visual recording."

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

The man appeared in the Tauranga District Court on Monday. A registrar confirmed to RNZ he had been granted interim name suppression and was placed on bail until his next appearance in September.

The man now faces an additional 21 charges of making an intimate visual recording.

Police confirmed on Monday the new charges relate to alleged recordings of adults.

RNZ has seen an email that has gone to parents from the early childhood centre on 6 July.

The email said the staffer, a full-time teacher, was arrested on 2 July.

"The matter remains the subject of an ongoing police investigation and we have been advised that this will take some time. We are fully cooperating with that police investigation.

"While the investigation is continuing, we do not know the full extent of the matter."

The email said all appropriate safety checking, including regular police vetting of the staffer, was undertaken.

"We know for some of you that this will come as a shock as he was a popular member of [the] team and well thought of by colleagues."

The Teaching Council register confirmed the teacher had voluntarily agreed not to teach.

Ministry of Education spokesperson Tui Rolleston earlier said the ministry was "supporting the service as needed".

"Given there is an ongoing police investigation it would not be appropriate to comment further."

Teaching Council chief executive Sean McKinley earlier said in a statement to RNZ that the safety and well-being of children and young people was "paramount to the Teaching Council".

"We can confirm that the Teaching Council has received a report regarding this teacher. Safeguarding learners is at the heart of the Teaching Council's role.

"When we receive information that raises concerns about a teacher's conduct or fitness to teach, we assess that information and consider what protective measures may be required under our statutory processes. These processes are designed to protect learners, prevent harm, and maintain public confidence in the teaching profession."

McKinley said that in general the Teaching Council was unable to provide information on complaints or Mandatory Reports that have been made to the Council.

World.title: Five Wellington sites could have heritage status removed or changed
World.content:
The government will consider changing or completely removing the heritage status of five Wellington sites to free them up for development.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop has also announced that he will also look at the height restrictions in the Courtenay Place heritage area.

The five heritage sites are the Karori Tunnel, Kelburn Viaduct, the former General Headquarters Building at the corner of Taranaki and Buckle streets, and the Miramar oil tank as well as those Courtenay Place height restrictions.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop RNZ / Mark Papalii

Bishop said that an investigation found some heritage provisions are having negative impacts on economic growth, and that modifying or removing them could enable around 770 additional apartments, generate $280 million in construction activity and support around 300 jobs.

The public can have their say on the proposals for 10 days from Wednesday.

"There are several statutory steps that must be completed before any regulations can be made. Wellington City Council has received the investigation report, and affected parties are now being invited to provide feedback on its findings," Bishop said.

World.title: CCTV shown at inquest into Isaac Levings' death after he fell in Wellington Harbour
World.content:
A Wellington court has been shown CCTV footage leading up to the moment Christchurch teacher Isaac Levings fell into Wellington Harbour and drowned in 2023.

Levings disappeared from Queens Wharf after attending a concert by pop rock band, The 1975 at TSB Arena in April 2023.

His body was found in the water near Te Papa two days later.

Presiding over the inquest into Levings' death on Monday, Coroner Katharine Greig said there had been more than half a dozen deaths involving people falling into the harbour since 2015 - including that of Wellington man Sandy Calkin.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Calkin's death - which was the subject of a previous inquest in 2024 - resulted in six recommendations to the council to improve safety along the waterfront.

Counsel for the coroner, Josh Shaw told the court the inquest into Levings' death was an opportunity to examine council progress on improving safety on the Wellington waterfront.

Shaw told the court the work to improve lighting along the promenade had been well advanced and proposals to improve edge protection had progressed towards public consultation.

"There was a will to continue this... and make sure that all that could be done was done to enhance safety at the waterfront," Shaw said.

Counsel for the coroner, Josh Shaw RNZ / Baz Macdonald

But he said a council proposal to proceed with edge protection measures near where Calkin had died and on the wider waterfront was voted down by council in August 2025.

"And so we are left, currently at least, with a waterfront with much better lighting - including at the Te Papa promenade where the lighting was not good at the time of Isaac's death - but has since been significantly upgraded.

"But a waterfront that has virtually no edge protection - at least across the majority of it. Including - because a couple of months after that August decision - there was also a decision to remove temporary fencing that had been installed pending a more long term solution," Shaw said.

Shaw said the inquest would examine the circumstances of Levings' death and also the processes by which the previous recommendations had "landed where they have".

A clever, quick witted teacher 'adored' by his students

Family of the deceased at the coronial inquest following the death of 25-year-old Issac Levings RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Today's inquest was attended by Isaac Levings' parents, Charles and Margaret Levings and his older brother James Levings.

Charles Levings described his son as a clever, quick witted and intelligent young man who was "adored" by his young students.

"At morning tea time, he was out on the field playing with the children - very rarely went into the staff room for morning tea - he would be out there on the fields. He understood children so much," Charles Levings said.

Charles Levings went to pains to express to the court that the level of intoxication illustrated by CCTV footage of the night of Levings death was out of character.

"For him to be intoxicated, as he was, was a surprise to me personally as his dad. I'd never seen him drink to that kind of level."

Isaac Levings' father Charles Levings at the inquest. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

CCTV tracks Levings along waterfront promenade

The Court was shown CCTV footage of Levings as he made his way south along the waterfront promenade after leaving the TSB Arena.

Levings could be seen in a stained grey T-shirt and shorts following a meandering path along the waterfront.

He posture was loose and he occasionally steadied himself against the wall and construction barriers along the waterfront edge of Frank Kitts Park.

Footage showed Levings crossing the bridge near the Taranaki Street diving platform as he walked along the Ara Moana walkway opposite Te Papa .

Soon after a splash and eddies could be seen on the calm surface of the harbour - emanating outwards from the wharfs edge at around 10.46 pm.

Daniel Bayliss went to the concert with Levings and some other friends that night.

He told the court the group had each bought ten packs of RTDs - consuming them before they arrived at the venue - and Levings purchased several more red wines as the concert progressed.

The Wellington waterfront moments after 25-year-old Issac Levings fell in 2023 RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said the last he saw of Levings was when he popped briefly into toilets as Bayliss was using them.

Bayliss said repeated messages and calls to Levings phone following that point went unanswered and unread.

Security staff member says she had 'a gut feeling' seeing Levings outside venue.

Louise Torres was working with the Red Badge security team at the venue that night.

She outlined the responsibilities and powers of the security teams stationed at the venue including being on the lookout for intoxicated concert goers and potentially evicting them from the venue as well as arranging transport or assistance for people deemed "at risk".

She said some time after 8.30 pm she was alerted to a concert goer with vomit on his shirt who turned out to be Levings.

"He had slurred speech, was unable to stand up straight and had bloodshot eyes," Torres said.

She said security staff supervised a chill out room where people might be taken, or go voluntarily, if they needed to sober up or "if they are feeling overwhelmed, too drunk or need to take a break".

Torres said she understood Levings' degree of intoxication would be assessed by paramedics or security staff in the chill out area.

Torres would later see Levings holding himself up on a pillar outside the venue but he "waived off" her attempt to speak with him.

"I remember thinking that Isaac still seemed drunk and having a gut feeling about him."

Torres told the court she later contacted police when she realised the same man she had interactions with was missing and told them she was concerned he had fallen in the water.

Wellington Free Ambulance Head of Event Medical Services and paramedic, Daniel Ashcroft told the court he was among six ambulance staff working at the concert.

Ashcroft said it had taken a wheelchair to assist Levings from the crowd but - in a better ventilated assessment room - and he was able to walk, talk and hold a conversation.

He said Levings had declined a more thorough assessment saying he had "only been drinking".

Ashcroft said he was called away to assist other patrons and on his return he was told Levings had been escorted out of the building by security staff.

"The reasons for his removal by security are unknown to me," Ashcroft said.

World.title: Wallabies to battle heat, typhoon in Japanese Test
World.content:
The Wallabies are not concerned Japan's searing heat and lingering typhoon will play a part in their preparation or Test match as they look to face old foes in Les Kiss's debut as coach.

Australia will take on Japan in the first of two Tests on Saturday night at Hanazono Rugby Stadium in Osaka, although conditions are not expected to be easy to play in.

Temperatures are tipped to stay in the high 20s to mid-30s degrees Celsius all week as the country grapples with a heatwave.

To make matters worse, Typhoon Dolphin is bringing wind gusts of up to 216kph and heavy rainfall ahead of hitting the Southern Japanese Ryukyu Islands on Friday, about 1,500 kilometres south of Osaka.

Wallabies thrash Italy as Schmidt era ends in triumph The Wallabies record a convincing 57-10 victory over Italy in Perth, as Joe Schmidt's coaching tenure finishes on a winning note.

But Queensland hooker Josh Nasser is treating the conditions as just another day in Australia.

"Obviously it's pretty warm over here, but I grew up in Brissy. We get some pretty hot summers as well. So humidity's up, temperatures up, but it's no different to some of the conditions we get back home," he told reporters on Monday.

"In the wet, the ball gets slippery, things tighten up a little bit. But I think we've got a big focus on just still trying to express ourselves.

"We play a fixture in Fiji each year, which we get pretty extreme conditions for.

"We're really not hyper-focused on it. We're just accepting that it will be hot, and then sticking to our processes."

Wallabies assistant coach Scott McLeod also warned of another typhoon that could affect Australia's clash.

"Is that Eddie Jones?" he joked when a journalist asked about Typhoon Dolphin.

Jones, who led Australia to a dismal Rugby World Cup showing in 2023 before resigning, will coach his second game against the green and gold with the Brave Blossoms.

Former Wallabies coach Eddie Jones will face Australia for the second time as Japan's coach. (AAP: Darren Pateman)

Nasser expects his presence to add extra spice to the fixture, especially as the master agitator took over the Japanese side just six weeks after resigning and was forced to deny that he had been in talks with Brave Blossoms officials during the World Cup.

Jones will not be the only Australian on the opposition, with former Queensland lock Harry Hockings along with Ben Gunter, Jack Cornelsen, Dylan Riley, Michael Stolberg and Tiennan Costley all options to play.

The Wallabies have been humbled by Australians featuring for different national teams in the past, most notably Canberra-born Mack Hansen when he scored a stunning first-half hat-trick to help Ireland win 46-19 last November.

"They'll be fired up to prove a point against us, I'm sure. [There's] nothing too strange about seeing them there, but it'll be a good battle," Nasser said.

"A couple of them are my good mates. Harry Hockings is one of my best mates.

"[I haven't spoken to him] on the rugby front, but I'm sure I'll catch up with him for a beer after the game."

The reunions will all culminate in Kiss's first match in charge of the national team since Joe Schmidt departed following the Wallabies' rousing 57-10 victory over Italy on July 18.

AAP

World.title: NRLW star in hot water for dangerous lifting tackle
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos NRLW star Ali Brigginshaw is facing the prospect of a lengthy stint on the sidelines after being referred straight to the judiciary for a lifting tackle during last weekend's Magic Round.

The Broncos remained unbeaten and on top of the ladder with a commanding 34-4 victory over the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs, but the win was soured by Brigginshaw's first-half tackle on Bulldogs halfback Tayla Preston.

Brigginshaw was sent to the sin bin after her tackle on Preston, where the Bulldogs player was swung around and lifted before being driven into the ground head-first.

Preston avoided serious injury, and Brigginshaw was handed a grade three dangerous throw charge.

The 36-year-old, who is playing her final season of NRLW before retirement, has never missed a Broncos game since the competition's inception in 2018.

She will argue her case at the judiciary on Tuesday, where she could face a significant ban.

Sydney Roosters forward Aliyah Nasio was the last NRLW player to be referred directly to the judiciary following a brawl at the conclusion of last year's grand final, where she struck Brisbane's Julia Robinson.

Nasio was banned for four matches after being hit with a grade three striking charge.

Brisbane, reigning NRLW premiers, faces Canberra this week, followed by a grand final rematch with the Roosters, then a derby against the Gold Coast Titans.

World.title: Canberra secures new NBL role amid expansion team hopes
World.content:
Canberra is one step closer to hosting an NBL team for the first time in more than two decades, the league's parent company chief executive has said.

The NBL's in-season competition, the Ignite Cup, will undergo a shake-up with the tournament's finals set to move from the Gold Coast to Canberra's AIS Arena.

It is the latest competition development in the nation's capital as speculation grows that the league is looking to expand into Canberra along with Darwin, the Gold Coast and a second Sydney team.

Ingles comes 'home' in coup NBL signing The legendary Boomers and NBA star will return to Australia's NBL for the first time since 2009, signing with Melbourne United for two years.

Competition executives have said they want to grow the current 10-team league, but new clubs will have to have the capacity to host at least 8,000 spectators.

With the ACT government announcing it will build the Canberra Convention and Entertainment precinct, hope remains the city can secure an NBL team for the first time since the Canberra Cannons were last involved in 2003.

The Cannons won three NBL titles before relocating to Newcastle, while the Sydney Kings now play some regular season matches at AIS Arena.

Admitting he would have loved to announce a Cannons rebirth on Monday, NBL Group CEO David Stevenson still gave every indication the league was eyeing the capital.

"We've got strong confidence that we can work together with Basketball ACT, with everyone involved in the sport to make sure that hopefully once the venue gets approved, that we can build a great team," he said.

"What we're building is a really strong business case, and it's not just about what happens at the game; it's the economic contribution that's really important for us."

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr added that a minimum of 7,500 seats were planned for the Canberra Convention and Entertainment precinct.

"A key element of the business case is having a basketball team play there, or more than one basketball team, actually. But it's not just a basketball stadium, it's got to accommodate other uses as well," Barr said.

"The AIS Arena is a fantastic venue, but it sort of maxes out at about 5,000 people.

"It was very clear in talking both to live music promoters, to the major sporting organisations … that we were missing out because 5,000 was too small."

But before expansion, the nation's capital will have to settle for the midweek Ignite Cup, an NBL competition involving 20 games held on Wednesday nights.

The four most successful teams will compete for a share in $550,000 when they progress to the semifinals in Canberra on February 19 before the decider on February 21.

The NBL's MVP Awards are also moving from Melbourne for the first time in more than a decade and will be hosted at the Great Hall in Canberra's Parliament House.

AAP

World.title: McIlroy headlines summer of golf with DeChambeau targeted
World.content:
The return of grand slam winner Rory McIlroy and the first Australian PGA Championship in Sydney this century highlights a 19-event summer of golf starting this month.

With the global professional golf scene in a state of flux, the Australasian Tour has secured a record partnership and announced a jam-packed schedule with major championship and European Tour spots once again up for grabs.

McIlroy back gracing Melbourne fairways, this time at iconic Kingston Heath from December 3–6, and the PGA Championship at The Lakes possibly featuring big-hitting fan favourite Bryson DeChambeau, are the two hottest tickets.

McIlroy completes one of his missions Rory McIlroy's appearance at the Australian Open in Melbourne has gone a long way to restoring the prestige of the tournament.

Record crowds followed the Northern Irishman at last year's Australian Open at Royal Melbourne before McIlroy successfully defended his US Masters title at Augusta National in April.

Officials revealed they were also targeting two-time US Open winner DeChambeau for the PGA, which was last held in Sydney back in 1998.

The new season begins in the now traditional style with the PNG Open at Royal Port Moresby Golf Club on August 27–30 before visiting all mainland states in Australia, as well as New Zealand's north and south islands, across the 19-tournament schedule.

The centenary Queensland PGA Championship will take place on the Kurrai course at Nudgee Golf Club in Brisbane from November 19–22.

Boasting a past champions list that includes Australian greats Greg Norman, David Graham and Peter Senior, the event will be played immediately before the Australian PGA Championship.

Co-sanctioned by the European Tour, the Australian PGA Championship also marks the start of the Race to Dubai, the tour's season-long rankings competition.

The PGA Tour of Australasia will also feature two new tournament venues in 2026–27.

Secret Harbour Golf Links, south of Perth, will host the WA Open for the first time, while Peninsula Kingswood Country Golf Club becomes the new home of Players Series Victoria as a forerunner to hosting next year's Australian Open.

There is a switch of order for the three-leg New Zealand swing in February that proved to be a huge success in 2026.

The New Zealand Open will now be the finale, following the Japan-Australasia Championship that returns for its second year at Royal Auckland & Grange Golf Club.
